subsubtopic: PENSIONS OF RETIRED WORKERS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Due to the fact that Canadian labour relations legislation does not permit the CNR union to negotiate pension rights for former employees, pensioners have had to put up with such measly increases as $77 over 19 years. This amounts to a grand total of $4 a year, or 33 cents a month, resulting in a $265 per month pension rate. A 33-cent increase does not go far against the odds of new record inflation rates of 12.6 per cent, 15.2 per cent increases in food costs, and 54 cents per gallon increases in gas prices. This is just one more Liberal-created national disgrace. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen):
That this House demands that the Minister of Labour immediately introduce amendments to Canadian labour relations legislation which would enable rail unions to negotiate on behalf of retired rail employees.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR INTRODUCTION OF BUDGET-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the government has abdicated all responsibility for controlling the rampant inflation which Canadians are experiencing today. The price of food eaten at home has increased 15.8 per cent. The price of fresh vegetables is up 73.5 per cent. The price of fuel oil is up 39.6 per cent. As always, those hardest hit are single parents, people on fixed incomes, women between the ages of 55 and 64, the working poor; in other words, those already struggling to make ends meet.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald):
That this House calls upon the Minister of Finance at least to acknowledge the punitive effect of these devastating inflation rates on Canadian women and introduce a new budget which will respond to this great tragedy.

speechtext:

Whereas some private Canadian citizens appear to have been involved in the planning, organization and financing of a recent plot to stage a coup against the legitimate government of Dominica, and whereas Canada lacks any legislative instrument comparable to the United States neutrality act designed to outlaw such plots and actions, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Hudecki):
That this House urges the government to bring forward legislation to prevent mercenary armies and other private citizens from using Canada as a safe haven from which they can launch armed activities against legitimate foreign governments.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In May, 1976, the then minister of finance doubled the allowable deduction for child care expenses from $500 to $1,000, acknowledging that the amount was too low in light of continuing inflation. Since then the cost of living has increased 56 per cent, leaving a 1976 dollar with a value of 64 cents. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling):
That this House direct the Minister of Finance to introduce a new budget before Parliament rises for the summer recess which would allow for total deduction of child care expenses from the income of a working mother or single parent.

subsubtopic: NEED FOR LONG-TERM POLICY-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity. The consumer price rise in April produced the highest year over year rate of inflation in Canada since World War II price controls were phased out in 1947-48. This has caused a rapidly accelerating rise in the entire cost structure of the fishing industry because of inflation, increasing fuel and energy costs, and high interest rates, placing this industry in jeopardy. Since there is today conflict between fishing interests for access to the resource, conflict between fishermen and buyers over price, conflict between government, processors and fishermen, and conflict between federal and provincial governments over control of the resource and the industry, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke):
That the government take steps immediately to establish a clear, long-term government-policy for the research, management and development of Canada's fisheries since the lack of a coherent policy imposes severe difficulties for managers and investors in the private sector.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In light of the malfunctioning of the pipeline constructed by Amax Ltd. to dump toxic mine tailings into the ocean at Alice Arm, B.C. and that two recent accidents have allowed toxic waste to be spilled into the sensitive intertidal zone, contrary to both federal and provincial legislation, and also that the interim report from the scientific review panel confirms that the government and Amax technical studies are inadequate to ensure environmental and health safety; and further, in light of concerns raised by the U.S. department of state regarding pollution of American waters from this operation, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar):

COST OF LIVING INCREASE IN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND AND NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:

Figures released today reveal that, except for Vancouver which has special and distinct problems because of its housing market, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland have suffered the highest annual increase in the cost of living in all of Canada. May 15, 1981

Madam Speaker, the Minister of Finance brags about his record as far as Prince Edward Island is concerned. The Atlantic provinces have the highest unemployment rate in the country, are being crippled by soaring interest rates, and now must face the second highest inflation rate in the country as a result of the very policies he brags about. speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):

It seems to me that, if he wanted to be fair, he would look at the very substantial investment that has been made by the Government of Canada, giving evidence of our interest in the welfare of the people of Prince Edward Island. I do not think that, on a comparative basis, any province in this country has been treated better or, indeed, as well as the province of Prince Edward Island.

subsubtopic: INVESTIGATIVE REPORTING BY RADIO STATION CFTR, TORONTO
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Communications. It concerns the way in which the Toronto radio station, CFTR, dealt with information it had on a group of mercenaries planning to overthrow the government of Dominica. The radio station claims to have learned about the plot last October, conducted taped interviews with the conspirators, but did not inform any authorities, because, as the station's news director, Robert Halliday, said:
If we'd gone to the police, we'd have had to work alongside them and then we wouldn't have had the story.
Since there seems to be a trend toward manipulated, sensational reporting these days, will the minister direct the CRTC to determine whether such so-called "investigative reporting" is consistent with the commission's regulations? speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the minister of energy who is being replaced in his seat by the government House leader, something which is long overdue.

subtopic: POSITION OF SINGLE WOMEN AGED 55 TO 64 YEARS
POSITION OF SINGLE WOMEN AGED 55 TO 64 YEARS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
The minister will know that Statistics Canada reported in 1979 that 41.5 per cent of single, divorced and widowed women aged 55 to 64 who did not live with relatives had incomes well below the poverty line. With today's running inflation and the escalating CPI, these figures are now much higher. These women, of course, do not qualify for the assistance available to senior citizens at age 65, and with unemployment at 7 per cent they have little hope of finding employment. My question to the minister is, will she introduce now as a short-term emergency measure special assistance to women aged 55 to 64?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: POSITION OF SINGLE WOMEN AGED 55 TO 64 YEARS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we are well aware of the problem of special groups of people under 65, and especially of people between 55 and 64 who must unfortunately survive only with provincial welfare benefits. Unfortunately, under the present distribution of federal-provincial responsibilities, the federal government ensures that married couples over 65 have incomes above the poverty line and we hope that we can soon do the same for single people. The provinces must take their own responsibilities. As I have said, with the present jurisdiction set-up, we cannot take direct action for the social welfare of people under 65.

subtopic: POSITION OF SINGLE WOMEN AGED 55 TO 64 YEARS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the women who are in that age group 55 to 64 will find themselves taking little comfort from the response that it is somebody else's responsibility. To see that these needs are met, and until such agreement can be made and the situation jointly dealt with through consultations with the provinces, will she urge her colleague, the minister responsible for employment, to introduce on an interim basis an employment incentive program specifically targeted for women aged 55 to 64 so they might have some opportunity to get short-term employment? How long are we going to go on saying to these women, "You have to live below the poverty line"?
[ Translation]

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: POSITION OF SINGLE WOMEN AGED 55 TO 64 YEARS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not think that the hon. member is doing anyone a service by speaking in this way. It seems to me that it is more important to give people information on which they can act and point out that, at the present time, the provinces-and they are well aware of this problem which we have often discussed at joint meetings-can decide to increase their welfare and assistance benefits, in which case we would reimburse automatically 50 per cent of this increase. I think that we should tell people to whom they should apply instead of playing games and pretending that we have certain
responsibilities when we do not. On the other hand, as to granting assistance to industry to hire women who have trouble finding employment because they are older and are unfortunately the victims of an unwritten prejudice, I would like to repeat-and I am happy to have the opportunity to do so-that in late January, my colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, established a program which should help to hire immediately and over a period of two years 4,300 Canadians including women in this age group who have difficulty in finding employment through normal channels. Under this employment incentive program, the employer receives 80 per cent at first, then 50 per cent and finally 25 per cent of the salary paid to such people. I invite women to make use of this program by going to our Manpower Centres.

subsubtopic: UREA FORMALDEHYDE-ADVISORY COMMITTEE'S RECOMMENDATION ON ASSISTANCE TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:

On April 23 of this year the minister banned urea formaldehyde foam insulation, and did so on the recommendation of a report from an expert advisory committee which she appointed in December. I would ask the minister when she intends to implement that recommendation, and what has she to say to those people who have been so exposed?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: UREA FORMALDEHYDE-ADVISORY COMMITTEE'S RECOMMENDATION ON ASSISTANCE TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext: What I can tell my colleagues in the House of Commons today, Madam Speaker, is that I have already the agreement of five provinces, if I recall properly, including New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Ontario-I seem to be missing a few-which have offered to help us to provide assistance. May 15, 1981

knows, that the board of health in the city of Toronto has indicated it has no information that is useful to it from the ministry which tells at what level it can predict there are difficulties in respect of exposure.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR DISSEMINATION OF INFORMATION IN TORONTO

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of State for Science and Technology. Given that Imperial Oil and other companies have indicated an intention to expand their research capabilities in Canada- and Imperial Oil particularly has indicated an expansion probably taking place in Sarnia and in Calgary-and given the fact that these projects are only going to go ahead on the basis of present legislation, particularly capital cost allowances, can the minister confirm that any changes to be made in the research and development policy will not in any way diminish the benefits which are presently available to corporations which are already embarking on building and expanding research facilities?

speakeroldname: Hon. John Roberts (Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: QUERY WITH RESPECT TO FUTURE CHANGES IN POLICY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for the question. As he knows, we have put forward what we think are effective and ambitious plans for government expenditure designed to help

May 15, 1981
Oral Questions
Canada's economy reach an over-all figure of 1.5 per cent of gross national product directed to research and development. However, it will not be by government efforts alone that we will be able to achieve our objectives, and we are calling for and hoping to see a very greatly increased expenditure on the part of the private sector. subsubtopic: APPLICATION TO LIQUOR SALES-PURPOSE OF INDEXATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. In his speech on May 6 last to the Conference Board of Canada the minister indicated that he supported Governor Bouey in his indication to Canadians that we can expect even higher rates of inflation. Can the minister tell this House how the indexing of tax to the consumer price index as it applies to commodities such as wines, beers and spirits is not in itself inflationary, and will the minister tell this House how he intends to fight inflation when he states that the real purpose of indexing taxation to the consumer price index is to prevent government revenues from eroding?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: APPLICATION TO LIQUOR SALES-PURPOSE OF INDEXATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member realizes that we will be dealing with this question at the report stage of the bill in due course, but just let me say as a preliminary that the purpose of this particular indexing is to achieve what a normal tax on value as a proportionate value would achieve. It does not in itself add to inflation. It is the equivalent of a tax based on an increased value of a commodity, and there are many of those taxes in our system.

subsubtopic: APPLICATION TO LIQUOR SALES-PURPOSE OF INDEXATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, if the intended purpose of indexing is to prevent government revenues from erosion, then will the minister tell us that he proposes to extend that indexing to other commodities and, if he does not intend to extend it to other commodities, how can he justify the continued discrimination against these products by indexing only excise tax as against wines, beers and spirits?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: APPLICATION TO LIQUOR SALES-PURPOSE OF INDEXATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the reason is that there is a different tax system, an ad valorem tax, on other commodities.

The House resumed, from Tuesday, May 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. Kaplan that Bill C-61, respecting young offenders and to repeal the Juvenile Deliquents Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Lawrence (p. 9497).

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was beginning to make some remarks the other evening when

May 15, 1981
Young Offenders Act
the bill was called. I would like to extend those remarks to pick up the thread of what I was saying earlier. In that speech I had been referring to the importance of the amendment and my concern that a whole day had gone by without having a response from the government as to the position the government might be taking on the amendment.
For the purpose of framing it, I want to say that the amendment filed by the hon. member for Durham-Northumb-erland (Mr. Lawrence), seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour), is one in which the House is asked to decline to give second reading to the bill at this time because the bill "rejects the fundamental principle of equal treatment of all persons before the law by specifying that the act will apply to different age groups in different provinces".
It occurred to me at that time, and I so mentioned to the House, that the application of the law would vary for offenders depending on where the offence occurred. Government members expressed Firmly during the constitutional debate the belief that federal laws and rights ought to apply equally to all Canadians. I am sure my friends remember those vehement statements made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien), the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) and others during the constitutional debate; and we ought to consider that if that is to be the ethos of the government, it ought to apply with respect to juveniles and young offenders. This is the opportunity to do that.
The answer from the minister was in the form of an interjection during the debate indicating that that had been the case for a long period of time; that under the Juvenile Delinquents Act there had been different laws applying differently across the country. I know that. That is precisely the problem. Now is the opportunity for the government to move in a way which could bring some uniformity to the law. That is the purpose of the amendment.
This is what we call a reasoned amendment. It is most unusual. You, Mr. Speaker, were in the chair at the time and I commend you on your judgment with respect to that. It is important at this stage to be able to zero in on principles that would apply so that debate becomes more relevant. This is one of those amendments which makes a debate relevant. It is a concern. As I mentioned, and as was mentioned by the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland, the law as it stands, with the exception of that particular matter, has the general support of this and other parties in the House.
When the minister introduced the bill on April 15, 1981, he made an excellent summation of what this bill is designed to do. The minister is in the chamber. I think it would be worth while to quote what he said. I quote:
The proposed legislation blends three principles. The first is that young people should be held more responsible for their behaviour, but not wholly accountable since they are not yet fully mature and are dependent on others.
That is an excellent, socially mature and socially conscious mixture of principles in arriving at the first principle of the bill, that there is a feeling that young people should be treated as individuals, not necessarily as extensions of their parents,
and that the parents should have no vicarious liability for the acts of their children.
I pause to say it is interesting that the Solicitor General, who is introducing this legislation with this principle in it, brought forward as a private member a bill which provided that parents should have vicarious liability. Having been in his portfolio for some time and having looked at the problem a second time, obviously a sober second look with ministerial responsibility made him decide that the principle he espoused in the House at one time ought not to be espoused here.
I agree with the proposition set forth in the bill that to treat young people otherwise, to treat them as extensions of the parents, is to deny them and society the atmosphere of rationality in terms of enforcement of the law. No one in this House of Commons would deny that social conditions, family conditions and other things affect the attitude, and therefore the actions, of young people and others in the community. It moulds their lives. They are subject to the environment. To take the position that the law ought to be cognizant only of those things would be to deny the matter of rationality, the rational decisions made by human beings when contemplating any act, legal or illegal.
In the first principle enunciated by the minister, he has blended those two questions quite well. I again quote the minister:
The second point is that society has a right to protection from illegal behaviour, even though committed by a minor.
It is important for us to remember that although the bill does away with the Juvenile Delinquents Act and lays on a new ethic, there is still the principle of the responsibility of young people in this particular piece of legislation. Taking into account the question of maturity, young people have a responsibility to recognize that they live within a society which runs by certain rules and broad principles which they must observe as they would expect others to observe when dealing with them.
Also the minister said:
The third point is that young persons have the same rights to the due process of law, natural justice and fair and equal treatment as adults, and that these rights must be guaranteed by special safeguards.
The minister concluded:
Thus, the bill is intended to strike a reasonable and acceptable balance between the needs of young offenders and the interests of society.
That third point is very important. The Juvenile Delinquents Act was passed in 1908. There have been a host of attempts to change that old statute. When one reads the section dealing with the offences, one will find that the most insidious and profound offences can be committed. If one is convicted of being a juvenile delinquent, various things flow from it. One principle of law which is denied in the Juvenile Delinquents Act is the right for people to be certain of that for which they are charged. If one reads the old statute, one will understand exactly how vague and wrong it is.
May 15, 1981

The principle which the minister discussed dealt with the question of due process in an admirable manner. The bill will cover only young persons charged with Criminal Code and other federal statutes and regulations offences. It will not cover breaches of provincial or municipal laws. It covers the law within the federal scheme, particularly the Criminal Code, which I think impacts most heavily on young people. There is provision for a formal type of court proceeding in a different kind of court. As set out in the bill, there is a right to legal representation at all stages of proceedings, and there is the responsibility of the youth court judge to make the right known to the unrepresented youth.
The courts have moved a great deal in the past few years. They have been more conscious of individual rights of the accused person who has not yet been found guilty. He is not guilty, just accused. Most offenders are deemed to be innocent until proven otherwise; there has been a consciousness of that right. This ensures that in the all-important proceeding brought against a person defined as a young person by this statute, the person will be represented and he has a right to be represented.
This bill was dealt with by the minister's predecessor, the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland, when he was solicitor general. Now it has been dealt with by the minister who has the honour of having this bill approved. It is modern, progressive and reasonable with respect to its approach to dispositions. There is a provision for sentencing when offences are found and for absolute discharges. There are very substantial fines if appropriate. Also there is the provision for restitution which has the potential of conveying to the young offender that there has been an offence and someone has been deprived of property. There can be some compensation for the deprivation an innocent person suffered as a result of a wrongdoer through the imposition of this restitution provision. It provides for compensation orders for loss or damage to property, loss of income or special damages which arose because of personal injury to the victim of the offence. It puts an obligation on the judge, when he is considering making such an order, to take into account the ability of the young offender to pay or to earn. There is a good, healthy balance in there. It indicates that when one breaks the rules of society and is so found to have broken those rules, there is some alternative to jail, to a juvenile home or to some other place where juveniles are sent. In the appropriate circumstances, the judge has the right to ensure the young person is dealt with in such a manner that he will have brought home to him the importance of his action and the impact of it upon his victim. Also he will have brought home to him the obligation he owes as a result and, it follows, the obligation which he owes as a citizen in a society which operates by the rule of law.
The provision for the community service order requires the young person to perform a specified amount of work. This is a very progressive and important movement in the law. It can also help the person who by his conduct indicated some lack of responsibility to society and the community, that is, in a situation where it would be adjudged that he could absorb the
Young Offenders Act
lesson and the importance of remembering the contribution he should make to the community by being a good citizen. He would not be before the court if he had been a good citizen. The judicial system relating to young people is expanding and opening up to a great degree. There is sufficient scope for a judge to consider additional conditions. All in all, it is an admirable piece of legislation.
I know the minister would not claim complete credit for it. He is the beneficiary of work which was done on it by his predecessor, as his predecessor was the beneficiary of work done earlier by former solicitors general.
In committee it will be the objective of our party to look at this piece of legislation from the points of view of the principle, the clauses and the provisions in it to see if it is possible to improve it. I hope the government will listen to the comments of members of Parliament, because they will be made with those points of view in mind. This is a piece of legislation which is long overdue.
I am honoured to have had the opportunity to speak for a few moments in this debate. I hope someone will follow me who will tell the House whether our amendment is acceptable and, if not, why not. Perhaps he or she could enlighten the House as to whether or not something can be done at committee stage during consideration of the bill which would make the amendment acceptable to the government, if it is not, so that there could be some uniformity in the application of the law.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) would permit a brief question.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
My question relates to the remarks he made the other day, which he touched upon again today, concerning a universal upper age limit for the cutting in of the Young Offenders Act. I think the most enlightened age is under 18. I would have wished that the provinces would agree to that age, but the financial implications for provinces which now have a lower age are tremendous. It is by and large a burden which the provinces would have to bear almost completely on their own.
What I want to ask the hon. member is whether he would be prepared to impose on the provinces from this chamber a change in policy in a matter which the provinces have deeply felt views which have such enormous financial implications for them?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not, nor have I ever been, privy to the discussions which have obviously taken place between the minister, his predecessors and the provinces over a period of years. I knew that those discussions had been continuing, and since there is now an amendment on the floor of the House by one party which proposes to amend

May 15, 1981
Young Offenders Act
the bill, which I gather is in a way that the minister would like, I put it to the minister a few moments ago that we might use a period of time during the course of the committee proceedings to approach those provinces which do not conform with the upper limit to see if there could not be some change of direction, given the fact that after these many years we have arrived at a new statute, which is a new departure and a new situation. It is in that sense that I raise this matter.
I do not think I could answer the minister's question as to imposition until I knew all the facts. I do not have those facts, but the minister does. Perhaps at the committee stage he might bring them forward so that we could deal with them. I do think that the principle is one which ought to be pursued and not forgotten by the minister. It is a principle which I do not think ought to be impaled simply on a matter of cost.
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, as a former solicitor general I welcome the presentation of this bill, this new Young Offenders Act, which will reform and replace the old Juvenile Delinquents Act. This bill has many good provisions and I will deal with some of them later. On the other hand, it has certain weaknesses which have already been referred to, but I would like to highlight a few of them in the hope that they will be dealt with in committee and corrected at that stage.
As hon. members know, this reform has been in the works since 1965 with the publication of the justice committee report on juvenile delinquency. That was the year I was first elected to this Parliament. In other words, this matter has been around for almost 16 years. The Juvenile Delinquents Act was passed in 1908 and it has received only very minor amendment in all that time, and no amendment at all since 1929. In effect, the Juvenile Delinquents Act that we have today is basically the same act which was passed in 1908. As everyone knows, there have been many social, political and economic changes in that time which have tremendously changed our society.
Following the justice committee report of 1965 the first young offenders act was presented, Bill C-192, which was introduced by a Liberal government in 1970. That bill died on the order paper before the 1972 election, after much debate and controversy. Following that, in the same year I was appointed solicitor general. Since I was extremely interested in the subject, I took steps to move ahead once more with this matter.
After a rather lengthy review with the provinces and interested individuals in the private sector, we published a new draft bill in July of 1975. Unfortunately, that proposal ran into strong opposition, especially from the provinces, and it failed to be enacted. I should point out that criminal law matters are the jurisdiction of the federal Parliament but that the delivery of social services falls under the jurisdiction of the provinces, as hon. members know. Consequently, this is an area of joint jurisdiction.
The criminal law which we pass for young people or which we apply to young people under the Juvenile Delinquents Act or the Young Offenders Act must be administered by the
provinces through their social service agencies or through other institutions coming under provincial jurisdiction. As was just mentioned, the costs of delivering these services are rather high. In the circumstances it is desirable that there be close co-operation between the provinces and the federal government on the enactment of any new legislation dealing with juvenile delinquents or young offenders. In any case, my attempt failed.
Other attempts were made by the Secretary of State (Mr. Fox) when he was solicitor general in 1977 and by the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence) in 1979. These attempts were also without success. Consequently, we welcome this bill and urge its passage.
Many private reports and studies have likewise urged such reform. I have before me an excellent book by Elliott Leyton of Newfoundland which is entitled "The Myth of Delinquency". There is also the report by Sharon Moyer with respect to diversion in the juvenile justice system. There are many others. These reforms are badly needed.
Approximately 50 per cent of chronic young offenders go on to the adult courts. In other words, they go on to adult crime. In some cases reforms at the provincial level-and I have in mind my own province of Quebec-are being held up or declared invalid due to the lack of enabling legislation at the federal level. As hon. members know, and as I have pointed out, enabling legislation is necessary at the federal level if the provinces are to go ahead with their legislation, their reforms, which depend on our basic jurisdiction in criminal law.
The basic reforms in this bill, which I welcome, are, first, the increase in the minimum age of criminal responsibility from seven to 12 years of age. It is complete nonsense to consider that a person seven years of age can be responsible for criminal action. It is true that people of the ages of seven, eight, nine and ten carry out behaviour which is anti-social, but it is certainly repugnant to me and many others in this country that they should be treated under the provisions of the criminal law. While we had proposed in 1975 that the age of criminal responsibility be 14, 1 think that a change to 12 years of age is a good compromise since it has the consensus of the provinces.
The second good provision of this bill is that all young people, from now on, will have the right to due process in the same way as adults. They will have all the safeguards that adults have when they are before the courts; that is, the right to legal representation, their rights being specified, the right to be informed of what sections of the law they have contravened, and the right to appeal. Many of these provisions are not present in the Juvenile Delinquents Act as it exists today.
Another important reform in the bill is the total elimination of provincial and municipal offences and the elimination of the offence of juvenile delinquency, which served as a general catch-all offence. Under this bill only Criminal Code offences and other federal criminal type statutes will be subject to the Young Offenders Act.
May 15, 1981

Another important reform in the bill which is welcome is that it provides for many alternative sentence measures, a wide range of dispositions which judges can apply to those who are found guilty under the act, including diversion from the system where that is considered to be the best way of rehabilitating the young person. This also includes restitution to the victims of crime. Community service is also included where appropriate.
Another excellent part of the bill deals with the provisions which would automatically destroy the criminal records of the young person who was found guilty under the Young Offenders Act if, after two or five years, depending on the offence, he committed no further offences. There would be no need to apply to the National Parole Board for the setting aside or destruction of those records.
The major weakness in the bill has been referred to before, but I want to emphasize it. It is the variation in ages which will apply across the country. I think we can see the nonsense of this right in the capital area of Ottawa-Hull. In Quebec, under the present law one is considered to be a juvenile up to the age of 18 years; but in Ontario one is considered to be a juvenile only up to the age of 16 years. Consequently, if two young people commit the very same type of offence, one committing it in Ottawa and the other committing it in Hull, the one in Ottawa would be tried in the adult courts and would perhaps be sent to Millhaven Penitentiary, while the one in Hull would be tried before a juvenile court and would perhaps get a probation order, be sent to a juvenile farm, or something of that nature. I think it is completely illogical-and as I say, it is blatantly obvious in this Ottawa-Hull region-that such variations in our dispensation of justice should take place in this country.
This bill proposes that the maximum age be 18 years, and that is the government's preference, but it is subject to be changed down to the age of 16 years if any province so requests. In many cases the reason the provinces give for not changing it to a maximum age of 18 years is the financial one. There were questions on that just prior to my remarks.
I negotiated with the provinces and dealt with that matter. I think the argument based on cost and expense is a red herring, because if one were to increase a maximum age for juvenile crime under the Young Offenders Act to 18 years, a lot of the expenditures for adult corrections in that province could be transferred to the juvenile system where it would have a much greater effect. Every expert that I know of who has worked in the juvenile and criminal justice system will say that if one is to turn around a potential criminal, the time to do it is when he is still young, not wait until he is 24, 25 or 30 years of age. Efforts should be concentrated on that person when he is first apprehended, when he first starts getting into trouble with the law. So far as I am concerned, to transfer money from the adult correction system into the juvenile system, with a maximum age of 18 years, is a much more reasonable provision. I personally have a private bill before this House, Bill C-253,
Young Offenders Act
which would bring about that very thing; but I tabled that bill before the minister presented this bill.
It is my hope that we can send this bill to the justice committee, of which I am a member, to explore ways of correcting this weakness in the bill. I know the minister wants to correct it as well. However, I reject the amendment of the official opposition, which would delay the whole process, the whole bill, and delay many needed reforms for a lengthy period of time. I think the better way of dealing with this is to send this bill to committee as quickly as possible and for the committee to deal with it there, attempt to discuss the matter with the provinces and, if necessary, hear witnesses from the provinces and so on. We should attempt to find a solution there rather than delay the bill.
I have seen so many delays with this particular bill. The provisions are all piled here on my desk: "Youth in the Law", Highlights of Proposed New Legislation for Young Offenders", "Legislative Proposals to Replace the Juvenile Delinquents Act", now the Young Offenders Act, and there are other bills that I do not have with me today. However, this review has gone on and on, as has been pointed out, for 16 years. Now is the time to resolve it and to pass the legislation.
There is another weakness that I see in the present bill, and that is the age of transfer to the adult court. In my provisions of 1975, it was suggested that a case could be transferred to the adult court when the offender was age 16 and it involved a serious offence. This bill provides that this should be done at age 14. I personally feel that 14 is still too young an age for one to be tried in the adult court. I know that there is no dogma on this matter, but my preference would be for 16 rather than 14 years of age.
My only complaint against the wide range of dispositions which, on the whole, are excellent is the maximum fine. I think this bill provides for a maximum fine of up to $1,000. I feel that for young people, especially if they are under 16 or even under 18 years, that is too much. Most of them are not working. If the fine is to be meaningful and if they are to pay it themselves, I would prefer a maximum fine of $200, or at the most $500.
I will have more to say on this bill in committee and perhaps at third reading, especially with respect to the situation relating to young persons, their special needs, and why we need special legislation and institutions for young offenders; but I will refrain from speaking on that for the moment. I would urge, however, that the House pass this bill on second reading today, if possible, and that it be dealt with in committee as quickly as possible so we can improve the legislation and pass it this year, after, as I say, a long journey of 16 years.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1, too, rise to speak on this bill which I consider to be a very important one. I get a chance to speak in this House often on oil prices and economic matters, but very seldom do I get a chance to speak on social matters. That is why I am particularly pleased to speak to this bill today. Often in the House that is the general trend, but that does not mean that the

May 15, 1981
Young Offenders Act
economic matters and those energy matters are the be all and end all of discussions in Canada. Social matters are just as important, especially when they concern young people, because, as we agree on all sides of the House, when dealing with young people and with children we are dealing with the future of our country.
I have a special interest in this bill dealing with young people and crime, having had my house in Ottawa broken into twice in the last two months, and I think juveniles were involved. I can share the concern that many people have in the country with the amount of juvenile crime, petty thefts, breaking and entering and so on. Any member who comes from an urban riding will hear from his constituents about the rather large numbers of offences of breaking, entering and theft which tend to involve juveniles. That is unfortunate.
I also have a longer term interest which goes back somewhat, as the first job 1 had as a lawyer was as the juvenile prosecutor for the city of Vancouver. I spent some time and learned my law in the family courts of Vancouver. 1 fondly remember those years. When the hon. member who last spoke, the former solicitor general, refers to all those reports, all the suggestions we have had for reform and change of the juvenile law, I know that frustration goes right down to all the social workers across this country, all the probation officers, childcare workers, clerks, judges, prosecutors, defence lawyers, and all groups involved in juvenile justice in Canada. Indeed, if one could ask them, I suppose the kids would reflect this as well.
This legislation that we have on the books right now goes back a long way, to 1908. That, in itself, shows the difficulty of getting change. It is hard to get change in anything, it seems, in this country. However, it seems to be particularly hard to get change in juvenile and children's legislation. All the people I have previously mentioned and governments are at fault here. We must get our act together and get change. The present Juvenile Delinquents Act goes back to 1908. That was a significant year. I think it was the year the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was born.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Another event that year which was of importance to was the fact that the present Juvenile Delinquents Act came into law. I say to the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan), who I see in the House, that the law was very progressive for 1908. Why? Before that time was the Victorian age when people, including juveniles, were hanged for petty thefts and crime. The law in 1908, as the Solicitor General knows, the present Juvenile Delinquents Act, dealt with juveniles as misguided children, to use the words of the act, "in need of aid, encouragement and assistance". So that was a very progressive act. I wish I could say the same of this act, and I will tell the minister in a minute why I do not think this is a progressive act for our time. I will offer the minister a suggestion for a really new juvenile system. I think we can set a couple of goals in a progressive juvenile system; we can protect society and the welfare of the child. Those two goals are not mutually exclusive.
There are some progressive measures in this bill, I acknowledge that. There is the end of the status offences and the opening of the juvenile court to the public, thus demystifying that court. There is the change in the age of criminal responsibility. There are some procedural safeguards for juveniles, such as the right to bail, access to counsel-although if counsel is not free, access does not mean very much. There are provisions for transfer of juveniles from juvenile court to adult court if the offence is serious, although those provisions are not adequate, and I agree with the previous speaker that they should be considered in further detail in committee. Having had the experience of going through hundreds and hundreds of transfer applications under the present law, I think that matter should be reconsidered.
The bill has one glaring flaw and the previous speaker put his finger on it. It does not acknowledge equality under the law. We really cannot have different age standards for, say, Hull and Ottawa, that a child be considered an adult and receive the full force of criminal law in Ottawa, but be considered a juvenile and receive the force of juvenile law, which is more in tune with the protection of the juvenile and reform, in Quebec.
I suggest that the hon. member who spoke previously is not only right but wrong as well. This bill should not go to committee; the government should bring amendments in now. As the bill now is written it does not make sense; it clearly violates the principle of equality as set out in the new charter of rights. It is ironic that the government, which argued against checkerboard civil liberties across the country, and the Conservative party, which seemed to favour it, are now on opposite sides. The government is bringing in a bill that will result in checkerboards, with a juvenile being under age 18 in Quebec, under 16 in Ontario and under 17 in British Columbia.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: That is the way it is now.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Yes, that is the way it is now. I suggest the Solicitor General has the power to change it. I invite him to bite the bullet. He knows this is right. He has heard what a former solicitor general had to say so he should do it. Make it a uniform juvenile age across the country.
Before I sit down, I want to congratulate the Solicitor General for funding a program in my riding which is really progressive called the community accountability program. It is carried out in Cedar Cottage, Kensington, which is an area of Vancouver bounded by Nanaimo, Broadway, Fraser and 41st Avenue. I see the Solicitor General nodding his head so perhaps he has acquainted himself with the program. Every politician and bureaucrat associated with juvenile matters visits the program, yet we had trouble getting the money to keep it going this year. I must say, however, that the Solicitor General has been good about continuing funding for the program, and with a little pressure the provincial attorney general also found some money for it.
May 15, 1981

Under the program, community accountability panels comprised of local citizens deal with juvenile offenders referred to them as a result of minor or summary conviction offences. The panel decides on the punishment, whether it will be restitution, payment of money to a victim, community work, or an apology. The panel, comprised of people from the neighbourhood, finds out what is happening with the family, with the child's education, and why the child is behaving in a certain way. It claims an 85 per cent rate of success and is starting to reach down into the community. This program is progressive and democratic, and it works.
The Bill before us today by contrast is not very progressive. Basically, it provides a criminal code for juveniles. There is some mention of diversion but it is really a criminal code for juveniles, as our NDP justice critic, the hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), said in his excellent speech.
Just before I was elected in 1979, I visited the small town of Sterling in Scotland. As a result of the Kilbrandon report of 1968 which dealt with children in trouble, there is in Scottish law a full system of community accountability panels such as the one we have in Vancouver. Ours in Vancouver is just an experiment and does not have the full force of law behind it. But in Scotland, any juvenile committing an offence or being accused of being a delinquent who pleads guilty-as 90 per cent of juveniles do-comes before a panel. If they do not plead guilty, they go to juvenile court, but if they acknowledge their guilt, they go before a panel.
I saw a panel at work in Scotland. A young boy called Allan had been sentenced to leave his family because there was a permissive grandmother in the family who got him into trouble. He was sent to another home and school out of town. When 1 was there he was back before the panel asking that his sentence be reviewed. The panel said, "Look, son, we'll give you another six months. You can come back and live with your Grannie in six months if it works out." They got a report from the probation officer and so on.
There was another case of a young girl who had been moved in order to get better schooling. There was a report that she was doing a good job. The uncle and aunt and one of the parents were present. The panel agreed to take her off probation and put her permanently in the home. The family agreed. This was a really progressive juvenile system that was working.
There are some good things in this bill, Mr. Speaker, but it is not progressive in the second half of the twentieth century to go back to a criminal code for children. I would like to see the government examine the experiment in Vancouver and think about establishing it for the whole country. What a new juvenile system we would have then! It is not just pie in the sky, so-called socialist idealism because the system is working in Scotland now. What works in Scotland must work! Being a Scot I can say that. It is an example of bringing juvenile justice back into the community where it belongs.
I want to conclude by quoting from the 1975 report of the National Council of Welfare entitled "Poor Kids" as follows:
To be born poor is to face a greater likelihood of ill health-in infancy, in childhood and throughout your adult life. To be born poor is to face a lesser
Young Offenders Act
likelihood that you will finish high school; lesser still that you will attend university. To be born poor is to face a greater likelihood that you will be judged a delinquent in adolescence and, if so, a greater likelihood that you will be sent to a "correctional institution". To be born poor is to have the deck stacked against you at birth, to find life an uphill struggle ever after. To be born poor is unfair to kids.
It was my experience in juvenile court that we dealt with poor kids, kids from single parent families, kids who never got a proper education or a proper chance.
The way to deal with juvenile crime is to deal with poverty first. The second way is to bring it right into the community and have neighbours deal with these problems; that happens in Scotland and in China.
I would ask the Solicitor General to amend the bill and make the situation all the same across the country, and when he brings in his next bill, to consider a really progressive system based on the Vancouver experiment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is nice to be debating another piece of legislation for a change. Bill C-61 is a very important bill, the Young Offenders Act, which is to repeal the Juvenile Delinquents Act. 1 want to congratulate our spokesman on this subject, the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence), who spoke in the debate on May 12, 1981. He has already discovered a number of major weaknesses in this piece of legislation. First, when young people run afoul of the criminal law they are not treated equally across the country. In this respect the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland introduced an amendment in an attempt to correct this, which reads:
That all the words after the word "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor: "this House declines to give second reading to Bill C-61, an act respecting young offenders and to repeal the Juvenile Delinquents Act, because the bill rejects the fundamental principle of equal treatment of all persons before the law by specifying that the act will apply to different age groups in different provinces."
It is ridiculous to have a federal law applied differently in each province. I am pleased that the Speaker has ruled the motion in order. We hope this amendment can be added to the bill. It will certainly be a major improvement to it.
I also want to congratulate my colleague the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid) for the contribution he made to the debate. As reported at page 9503 of Hansard, he said:
While I am in large part in support of the bill, I cannot accept the position of the Solicitor General that we must rush through the debate at second reading.

May 15, 1981
Young Offenders Act
We certainly cannot be rushing the bill through because we have found in it quite a number of weaknesses. We want to highlight these weaknesses first before sending the bill to committee.
The basic purposes of the act are, first, that young offenders are given more responsibility for their actions. Second, they have been given stronger rights under the law. Third, there is greater flexibility and, therefore, a greater chance of rehabilitation under the law.
There are still some very vague points in the bill. Clause 3 makes allowance for young offenders to settle out of court instead of having a day in court, but no guidelines have been set for this process; as an example, there is nothing which states for which crimes this can be done, who deciphers punishment and how it will be enforced. In addition, Clause 20(1) gives a judge ten distinct courses of action in sentencing. Clause 11 is a grandfather clause which allows the judge to do just about anything he wants.
Within the measure there is a uniform minimum age stipulated which has been agreed to by eight out of the ten provinces and all speakers to date. However, there is no uniform maximum age set for young offenders. This creates a checkerboard effect across the country as some provinces will have one maximum age and others another. That is why I hope the motion of my colleague, the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland, will be accepted by the Liberal Party and New Democratic Party. The bill creates inequality throughout the proposed measure.
The maximum fine for young offenders is $1,000, but for people under 18 this is quite a high figure. We would not want to promote more crime to pay for past crime. We are experiencing serious youth crime in the country today, and part of the reason, or perhaps the main reason, is the high unemployment rate for those from age 15 to 24. There is serious concern across the country about juvenile crime. 1 have received some letters very critical of the government, our jail system, our bail system and the weak punishments we have in respect of many of these serious crimes. I should like to read a portion of a letter from a concerned citizen of British Columbia. He points out:
-a boy is castrated in a public washroom in Clearbrook, B.C. by two juveniles. The juveniles are apprehended and released after questioning. Another boy is castrated by the same two juveniles. What is your answer to this boy and his parents-
He directed that question to me and all other members of Parliament. He wants to know what we are doing by letting people like this out immediately after the commission of a crime as serious as that.
Here is another example this Canadian citizen has written about:
-a sixty year old lady is robbed at knifepoint and later raped by a seventeen year old youth. This man was never even charged for his action.
He points out in his letter:
Our members of parliament are safe and secure and don't give a damn about you. You embarrass the public image of the criminal and we don't want to know about your problems.
That is one example of how some citizens feel about our easy bail laws, letting these people off with light sentences, giving them a little slap on the wrist and what have you.
1 have with me a recent article from The Toronto Sun under the heading "Nurses cried at seeing raped girl". It states in part:
Police plan to petition the Wayne County Juvenile Court to have two 16-year-olds tried as adults in the rape-beating of an 11-year-old girl.
Nurses at Children's Hospital cried when they saw the girl, who suffered a skull fracture, stab wound to the chest and repeated slashes with broken glass.
"It was horrible .. . Those guys really wanted to kill her."
The girl, who lived on welfare with her mother and four brothers and sisters, was raped, beaten, kicked, stabbed in the chest and cut with broken glass for two hours Saturday night-
What is happening in the country today when we have youth committing horrendous crimes like this? It is important that we make improvements in our educational system. We must make students aware of how the law will deal with them when they commit serious crimes such as this. I do not know how many schools take their students on visits to jails, but this might help to some degree. It might not hurt to bring the paddle and the strap back to help them understand. Maybe then we will not have 11-year old girls being raped and elderly women attacked.
In addition, I am receiving many letters these days, as I am sure are all members of Parliament, in respect of the government's proposed legislation which would decriminalize possession of marijuana. I think public opinion is changing on this issue right now. I suggest today that if any surveys were taken the majority would oppose decriminalization of the possession of marijuana. Their concern results from so many young people getting on drugs today and committing serious crimes.
I have received a number of letters and documentations from the educational system across Canada, universities and schools. They are very concerned about any steps to decriminalize possession of marijuana. They feel all that will do is increase youth crime. I want to read some paragraphs from some of these letters from our educational directors across the country. This one states in part:
We are expressing the concern of 12 organizations closely related to the education of youth. We believe that if changes are made to this legislation which do not clearly impress upon society that the use of this drug is not condoned, there will be a significant increase in drug use, particularly by young people.
This letter goes into detail about the use of cannabis by students and young people. It states:
The use of cannabis by the students and young people of our country is a matter of urgent concern.
Representing, as we do, 12 provincial organizations directly involved with education and supervision of adolescents, we are perhaps more aware than most other groups of the harm already inflicted on our society by cannabis and other street drugs.
We are discussing the new Young Offenders Act and the difficulties we are having with youth in our courts today and in
May 15, 1981

society, and our educators who are living with these problems at first hand in the schools, the people who can advise us better than anybody, suggest that if we go ahead with the decriminalization of marijuana we could be opening up a real hornet's nest in Canada. If the government is planning to introduce such legislation in the near future, we will certainly have to call these educators as witnesses to advise us on how this measure will affect Canada's youth across the country.
In addition, I have received a resolution of the Nova Scotia Federation on Alcohol and Other Drug Problems which opposes the decriminalization of cannabis. I would just like to read one or two quotations from this document. They point out under the heading "Increased hazard to the young":
-marijuana is particularly dangerous to young people, as their bodies are not fully developed. A great many young people use marijuana, and it is only now that the dangers are becoming apparent. The full consequences may not be seen until our next generation, as was the case with Thalidomide. There are numerous other dangerous effects, such as chromosome damage, reduced defence against brain and liver damage.
This organization then presented a resolution to us as parliamentarians as follows:
Therefore, be it resolved that the Nova Scotia Federation on Alcohol and other Drug Problems requests the Department of Justice of the Government of Canada, and other appropriate bodies concerned, to take whatever necessary steps are appropriate to ensure that the current legal status regarding the use of cannabis remains unchanged, and that the Government of Canada and other concerned bodies seek the introduction of measures which will decrease the use of cannabis in Canadian Society.
We are dealing with a young offenders bill and at the same time the government is talking about decriminalizing marijuana. These documents received from the educational system point out that this will create nothing but problems for us. It seems that once a young person develops a drug habit it becomes an extremely costly habit, and so many of them have to return to crime, robbery, rape and what have you.
Since we have a very serious problem on our hands, we will not be able to rush this bill through, as suggested by the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan). That suggestion indicates to me that the minister does not understand the magnitude or the seriousness of the problem. This bill is a 90-page document, and we will have to go through it with great care because of the serious problems we have today with respect to juvenile delinquents, young offenders, drugs and crime. We shall have to go into a great deal of detail in the committee in dealing with this bill. We shall have to call in the police, the medical profession and so forth, which could contribute greatly to the improvement of Bill C-61.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all may I say to the House what a great honour it is for me to comment on a significant piece of legislation, an act respecting young offenders and which will repeal the Juvenile Delinquents Act. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, as the member for the riding of Mont-real-Mercier, I have had the opportunity to make frequent
Young Offenders Act
visits to the institutions where juvenile delinquents are housed, institutions such as Boscoville, Mont Saint-Antoine and the Cite d'accueil de la Riviere-des-Prairies.
Mr. Speaker, those institutions in my riding have enabled me to be in regular contact with youths in trouble with the law and with the professional staff responsible for helping them rehabilitate and become worthy citizens. I want to salute those professionals and I hope that the new bill will make it possible for all offenders, particularly the young, to turn over a new leaf and, finally, to enjoy a better life in a country such as Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to reply to some of the remarks made by members opposite, particularly by the former solicitor general, the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence), who said that the House had been waiting long for this bill. If I may, Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to make a slight correction and point out to hon. members that Bill C-61 received first reading last February 16 and was given second reading consideration on April 15, May 12 and again today. Therefore, less than a year after the election, the Liberal government introduced this important social measure and 1 am proud to take part in the debate on this bill. The hon. member for Huron-Bruce (Mr. Cardiff) as well said that the bill had been long in coming. Again if I may, Mr. Speaker, I would point out that the previous government had not introduced a bill as such in the House, all it did was to draft a policy statement. Having drawn inspiration from all existing documents, from reports prepared by government officials and from discussions held with the provinces, we suggest that perhaps this bill reflects the closer agreement between the provinces and the federal government since the provinces are partners in the administration of this legislation. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I take the liberty of reminding my colleagues that there would be no future for this statute without the participation of the provinces, for its administration falls under their jurisdiction.

I would like also to provide a clarification for the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Jarvis), who was asking the government about the difference between responsibility and accountability, two words we see in clause 3 of the bill. Perhaps I can offer a small explanation by saying that responsibility relates to capacity to form the intent to commit a criminal offence. According to the proposed Young Offenders Act, a young person would be responsible for his or her illegal behaviour, but she or he would not be held accountable in the same degree as an adult. That is why there will be different courts and different procedures for young offenders than for adults, and that is why we can say that responsibility and accountability are two different things under this bill.

Mr. Speaker, my colleagues have made several comments on alternative measures. I would like to explain in detail the avenues open to a youth in trouble, to a young offender. On the first offence, if it is a minor one the police officer can

May 15, 1981
Young Offenders Act
simply reprimand the young person and point out that his behaviour is reprehensible, and the procedure can stop there. On the other hand, at a later stage, perhaps for more serious offences, section 4 points out that alternative measures may be used. These measures are voluntary and the young offender can call on a lawyer at this stage to determine whether or not he can agree to the alternative measures. Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that at no time is there a question of pleading guilty to make use of these voluntary measures, and that moreover, the act specifies that even the statements made at that time cannot be held against the young person.
A later stage, Mr. Speaker, which is somewhat more serious, will allow law enforcement authorities, that is the provinces, to refer the young person to a youth court. At such a time, as my hon. colleagues have pointed out, the young person must have the assistance of a lawyer, and in fact, this right is clearly recognized in the legislation.
On the other hand, many means are available to the court to determine, if the young person is found guilty, what measures should apply to him, and I believe that several of my colleagues have noted how these measures or provisions will allow the young person to mend his ways.
However, Mr. Speaker, in extremely serious cases, or at the last stage, for a really hardened young offender, for a young person who may have committed several offences, our bill provides for the possibility of referral to an adult court.
Mr. Speaker, for the information of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro), and especially of my colleague for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) who spoke about remission or the state of mind that a young person must have concerning his offence and the possibility of restitution of the stolen or damaged goods, I would like to point out that we have included in sections 20(c) and 20(f) provisions through which the young person will have to compensate any person who may have suffered damage, loss or injury, or to pay a fine, as provided in paragraph (c).
However, what is important to point out to my colleague is that this legislation provides for restitution, but not necessarily with the parents' money, and thus may force the young offender to face his responsibilities. One of the major principles of this legislation is to force the young offender himself to make some type of restitution according to his means by services to the community.
My colleague mentioned earlier the possibility of paying back that money. 1 believe that it is not the intention of the legislator to force a young person to pay back the amounts in question which he may not have or to force him to commit another offence to do so.
Some hon. members, such as the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) and the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour), talked about vicarious liability. This is an option that was examined very carefully. However,
we have concluded that it would be difficult to adopt this option within our law. Civil law is the responsibility of the provinces. The application of this concept would involve great difficulty in terms of jurisdictional responsibility between the provinces and the federal government.
If I may give an example, a young person may be involved in a crime, such as a fire. The young person or the parents could be held liable for $100,000 damages, for instance. I do not think it is the intent of the legislators to be so extreme. I think the bill covers most cases in terms of restitution, or at least ensures that the young offender fulfils his responsibilities.
The hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) stated that clause 56(3) made the bill too lax with regard to evidence. I wish to clarify this point. It may be a misunderstanding that will be clarified at the committee stage. It is not the intent to collect evidence in a fashion which will place the young offender in a worse position than an adult. I refer to the situation where a young person may say to an arresting officer at the scene of a crime that he is guilty. It is not the intent to ignore such facts, but to recognize that later the young person should have the full protection of the law.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman) was concerned about the destruction of records. He said that if these were computerized, it would be difficult for the young offender to ensure that the records are destroyed. The bill does not provide that the information be sealed after five years but completely destroyed. The bill provides that when a young person becomes an adult he may make a special request for destruction of his records. He or she is probably the best person to know where the records are held and to ask that they be destroyed. It is very clear in the bill that it will be an offence for anyone to use the information. That is a safeguard to ensure that no records are used against the young person. This section, which was not in the previous act, can be improved and will be discussed at the committee stage.
The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) said that the rights and freedoms granted to the young person in the bill do not balance the responsibilities of that person. I remind the hon. member that the first principle of the bill is to see that the young person has the responsibility for his or her offence and will be held accountable before the court. This bill does not in any way remove the responsibility from the young person. Under this bill there will be more responsibility than under the previous legislation.
With regard to the family, clause 3(g) provides that the parents will be requested to appear before the court. However, the family is recognized as having the first responsibility in caring for the young person and should be there when the young person has some difficulty.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to add some comments as several colleagues have spoken of the problems related to the financial provisions of legislation. We do indeed recognize the fact that the addition of new rights, such as the right to counsel, will add to the provinces' expenses.

We are in fact negotiating with them at the present time and there will be a federal-provincial conference in June, which will be a follow-up to the round of negotiations which were held with each individual province. We do believe that, as a result of these discussions, financial arrangements for the new services will be worked out and also that an agreement will be reached between the provinces and the federal government. Therefore, I do not think there is any need to be overly concerned about additional expenses as discussions are well under way. I also think that so far none of the provinces has appeared overly concerned about the federal contribution to the new service.

I now wish to address some of the main objections of the opposition. Their position was set forward in the amendment of May 12. Most members who addressed that issue talked about the principle. The hon. member for Winnipeg-Assini-boine (Mr. McKenzie) talked about equality before the law. Let me state a few facts. First, the situation is that there is no uniformity in the application of the Juvenile Delinquents Act. This was outlined by some members.
The bill states that a young offender is a person of at least 12 years of age and not having reached the age of 18 years. There is provision for the provinces to lower the age. We agree with members opposite that the ideal situation would be a uniform age. However, as stated previously by the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan), there are cost factors involved. Certain services should be available, and at this time it might be a burden the provinces could not take on in order to implement the new act. The fact is that the age would be 18 in terms of uniformity. Upon request by a province to the federal government, it could be lowered. If no provinces were requesting a change, the age would be 18 across the country.
I would like to talk about the principle in terms of age by referring to a neighbouring country which has a federal system. The jurisdiction over juvenile delinquents lies with the state government in the United States, while our jurisdictional position is a mixed one, with the provinces having the right to administer the bill and the federal government having the right to apply this bill based on the Criminal Code. Recently in the United States there were 33 states using 17 years of age, 12 states using 16 years of age and some using 15 years of age. On April 9, 1981, the state of Illinois described the word "minor" as meaning a person under the age of 18 years. So one of the latest pieces of legislation in the United States refers to 18 years of age.
Also I should like to refer to the state of the international law. New Zealand uses ages 14 to 17; Australia, from 10 to 16; Japan, from 14 to 20; in Belgium it is under 18; England is from 10 to 18.
Clearly it is not a matter of principle. If it was a matter of principle, how could a country such as the United States with its first amendment, which is equivalent to our charter of rights, permit the young offenders bill to apply to 16-year-olds
Young Offenders Act
in some states and to 18-year-olds in other states? The point is very clear; it is a matter of administration by the provinces. Some provinces have indicated very clearly that they would prefer 16 or 17 years of age. Others are indicating that 18 years of age is a prerequisite to the adoption of this bill.
By stating its position on 18 years of age, the federal government is actually following current international law and showing some guidelines which could perhaps be followed in the future. There might be a period in which the provinces would adjust themselves to the 18 years of age principle. There will probably have to be some negotiations in terms of implementing an older age in some provinces. As we know very well, the treatment of juveniles and older persons before the adult court is quite different. It is a sociological fact that some provinces want a younger age and others want an older age. The amendment cannot be accepted based upon the question of principle; it is an administrative question.
By enacting this bill, we are taking a step in the right direction. We are tabling a bill for which the people in the milieu have been waiting some time, and I am proud to have participated in its debate.
