Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have an opportunity to participate in the debate on this bill. In its form, it is much similar to the one tabled on October 26, 1979 by the then solicitor general, the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence). If I may, I want to indicate my concurrence with the theme of the bill and its direction, that of ensuring young people are held more socially accountable, and are seen as individuals and not just as extensions of their parents.
In light of my experience in community relations and counselling, I welcome the thrust of a number of the proposals of the bill, such as the increase from seven years to 12 years for criminal responsibility. It more accurately reflects the maturing process of young people in educational theory. Also I welcome the right of due process of the law in the same way that adults have today and the elimination of a criminal record if after one offence a young person, as is often the case, finds himself rehabilitated and there are no further violations. Also there is the option of alternative sentences. In a day of rising expenses and when a great deal is spoken about the perpetuation of crime by criminal institutions, this is a very humanizing and responsibility-building mechanism.
In supporting the thrust of the bill, I also wish to indicate my reservation, as indicated in the amendment of the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland, that this matter of a uniform age for young offenders across the country must somehow be dealt with. In the processes of government, when things are left to be dealt with administratively, all too often we find that these things are perpetuated in the form in which they were passed.
As I look after the representations in the similar area relating to family law and the representations across the country in terms of support payments in divorce situations, I have found that women's groups have repeatedly indicated

May 15, 1981
Young Offenders Act
that they cannot accept the matter of each province making its own rules. We are looking at the reality of mobility in Canada, not only of spouses who may avoid support, but of young people moving across the country often in search of work. When they are unemployed, all too often they fall afoul of the law. The amendment correctly addresses the situation of the mobility of our young people at the moment.
Therefore, it is an important principle that there should not be different rights in different parts of the country, but that there should be uniform rights for all young Canadians across the country.
I would like to add some supportive and interpretative comments on one specific clause of the bill, Clause 22. It is closely connected with a number of initiatives that have taken place in my constituency. It is the provision for the option of a community service disposition in lieu of incarceration. This option has been used for over two years in the Kitchener-Waterloo area, beginning as an experiment under the guidelines of Sections 662 and 666 of the Criminal Code respecting probation orders, to the point where there are now some 280 community service orders being carried out in my region. Ranging in terms of 100 to 150 hours, the community service orders provide an invaluable learning experience for young people as an alternative to a jail sentence. These have proved especially effective for first-time offenders, since the emphasis of these community service orders is on the development of responsibility for one's action as opposed to gainless punishment.
Community service orders have been used frequently in the case of young people since with rising unemployment there have been more and more young offenders coming before the courts. Many cases involve breakdown in family life where parental guidance is lacking. This option is an extremely important part of this bill because it changes the emphasis from an isolated individual against the community, someone who is in a sense shaking his or her fist at the community, to someone who is in support of society and working on its behalf. This is accomplished through a positive contribution to the community, providing a service which would not otherwise be available in the community, which results in an exercise of socialization or reconciliation.
This option has been received into the cultural mosaic of Waterloo county, where there has been a tradition of community service. Therefore, this concept can be understood. Under community service orders services have been rendered to municipal governments, school boards and social agencies. In many cases they provide for the development of new skills. In a sense they provide training in trades. They prepare individuals to be able to offer something to the employment market while not competing with existing jobs at the same time. That is to say, community service orders are for volunteer work, an area of endeavour on which people in my riding place a great deal of importance.
One of the agencies which has benefited from this option is the victim-offender reconciliation service which has been pioneered by the Mennonite community in my area. This program encourages an individual to accept responsibility for his or her action, not with patronizing treatment for young people but by stressing reconciliation over punishment through the direct confrontation of the victim and offender. This service brings these people together to discuss their feelings and what must be done in order to close the gulf which has been created.
The John Howard Society in the Waterloo region is the agency which monitors the terms of a community service order. The society stresses that the terms of a CSO must be very clearly set out so that the offender understands that it is not a reprieve but rather an opportunity for that young person to regain a responsible and respected status in the community. These projects range from parkland clean-ups to giving assistance in senior citizens' homes. Again, the importance is that the service can only be provided by voluntary agencies, if at all. The effect of these orders is to get the community involved in corrections. They educate the community as to who, and not what, an offender is so that the community sees that it has a stake in its parts. Indeed, in a sense it is a socializing exercise. There is another agency called Youth in Conflict with the Law which was formed to try and bridge this gap. It has been seeking to socialize the whole tragic experience.
We are all familiar with a war situation where the aim is to depersonalize the enemy so that he or she can be seen as "it". This is done so that somehow the obliteration of the person, the dismissal of them, can somehow become more conscion-able. The idea of a community service program is rather to personalize the offender, to somehow show that he can make a contribution to society. In December I received a letter which reads as follows:

Mr. Speaker, speaking on this bill takes me back many years to when 1 was practising law. Although I did not specialize in the field we are discussing today there was always great discussion among practising lawyers about many of the difficulties in dealing with young offenders. At that time the circumstances were much different from what they are today. The mere fact that it has taken this long to present this bill makes us realize just how much difficulty there has been in agreeing on some changes. It is not a subject which has necessarily been dillydallied with; there are honest differences of opinion.
I can say that I do not share all the views of my colleagues on this question with regard to uniformity of age. 1 would have preferred to see the age limit set at 16. One should consider crime statistics today and the activities of young persons aged 16 and 17. Read your newspapers. What are they guilty of? They are guilty of some of the most violent crimes. They are not crimes which are, as suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), induced by poverty. Not a bit of it! There are any number of reasons why these young 16 and 17-year-olds are engaging in this level of crime. One reason, I suppose, is the dropping of the age of majority to 18 years. It was always said, when 21 was the age required to get into the beer parlour, that one saw 18-year-olds and 19-year-olds trying to get in. Then when the age was dropped to 18, the 16-year-olds were trying to get in, something that they could not do before.
Young offenders have no particular preponderance at any level of society. There are just as many young punks-and that is all they are, vicious-minded young punks-coming out of the best homes as out of the worst homes. The reasons that they have become like that are a reflection on today's society.
Rather than say that young offenders are the result of poverty, I would say that they are primarily the result of the lack of parental supervision and guidance. This is found par-
Young Offenders Act
ticularly in the higher income groups where attention or participation in raising teenagers is limited to giving them $20 to $50 on a weekend whilst the parents go off on their own to do their own thing. How many homes do hon. members know of where the way of dealing with their youngsters-as the father and mother are too often pursuing their own pleasures-is to turn over the keys to the family car, give $50 and say, "Have a good time this weekend, son. Just go around our high schools and find out how many kids, unfortunately, have that poor level of parental upbringing. That is where you get the start; but it goes on. Kids, from muppets to adolescents, have been watching television, with violence at all levels, even in the cartoons. In the pictures at which they look there is nothing but more and more violence. They become inured to it. They think it is great. After all, it is a reflection of society. They think, as they grow and see this continue, that this is society.
Naturally, at all times there are those who, because of poverty, go out to get a few dollars. However, I would say that they are, by far, the infinitesimal minority today. This leaves the further group, and I think it is the biggest one. These people, in order to satisfy their appetites for alcohol and drugs, go out on hold-ups, thefts, break-ins and purse snatching. Oh, of course, as my colleague, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) says, there is also the thrill of taking someone's car, just borrowing wheels, to see who has the fastest and raciest car, to see how much rubber can be burned and to see if someone else can be made to look like a chicken on the street. I suppose, in the end, in the words of the social worker, it really comes from peer pressure to be more outstanding than the others.
Those are the motivations, the reasons we have young offenders. It seems to me that to say that all persons under the age of 18 and over the age of 12 shall be lumped together as young offenders is totally wrong. I say that I would favour those attorneys general of the provinces who would opt to have those under age 16 put in the group of young offenders. With respect to the others, one only has to go in the courts to see whether the 16-year-olds and 17-year-olds are any different from the 18-year-olds or the 19-year-olds. I regret to say that in the great majority of cases, this is not the case.
Having said that, I do not think that the present penal system in this country is the one which will deal with this particular problem. We can go through legislation that we pass in Parliament, bill after bill, and say, "Jail for the offender". My goodness! There are offences with regard to agricultural chemicals where the penalty is jail. There are all sorts of offences for which jail is the answer. It is not the answer in these cases, and I appeal to my colleagues here. If we are going to spend money wisely in the administration of justice, then we should spend it on the prevention of crime where it arises, that is in the early years. That is where we should spend our money.

That is where we should spend our money with social workers and parole employees. We should not put first offenders into jail. They should be put on probation after a period of good behaviour during which they report to a parole worker.
Several hon. members suggested community work, the parliamentary secretary among them, and our colleague, the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean); alternatives where these young people can be put to work. There are so many things. I do not mean to suggest raking leaves, cleaning streets, or demeaning work of that nature. There are all sorts of good community work which they can be given to do.
1 fully subscribe, too, to the principle of restitution wherever it is possible. I do not believe a fine should be paid to the state. What will the penalty do? What about the dear old lady whose purse has been snatched and most of her cash taken? A young punk is picked up, and there is no doubt about his guilt. Then he is fined rather than sent ot jail. The state benefits as a result of the compensation it receives for apprehending him. A law-abiding citizen has a right to be protected by the state- she has that right, that is all she has; she gets nothing out of it. It is an empty letter. The same applies to the elderly couple or any person who finds their home broken into and things stolen. They may be covered by insurance or they may not.
1 am glad that judges in young offenders courts will now have the opportunity to use alternative methods of dealing with such situations. But we are really going to have to provide them with a framework that is well thought out and well administered so that young people can be put on their good behaviour-on a leash. How tight or loose that leash shall be, will depend on the skill of the parole worker.
There has sometimes been a problem with the place where young offenders are held prior to their court appearance. All too often it has been the overnight tank of the local police station. In large cities, many are found in the nightly run in the bullpen or in the remand centre where hardened criminals and young first offenders are put in all together. Sometimes the young ones glory in this because they are close to the feet of hardened professional criminals; it is something they can boast about to their peers in later days. The money must be spent where it will do most good.
A similar instance in recent times was the recycling of scores of thousands of public servants into second language training. That was like spreading a thin film of water on a desert. Had that money been spent wisely on teaching our children a second language, we would have had some brighter prospects for the future.
It seems to me that it is wrong to spend so much money every day on incarcerating thousands upon thousands of hardened criminals. Surely a lot of those people would not have become hardened criminals if they had been handled differently at the outset of their unfortunate careers.
I was struck by some particular features of this bill, Mr. Speaker. I should like to refer to clause 3 in particular, the
declaration of principle. Some people claim that there is a lot of "do-goodism" in this and that a lot of it is a cliche. Some of it is obvious, but I think that as a general body of policy for this country to adopt toward its young offenders, it is a step in the right direction.
One thing is badly lacking, however. In subclauses (l)(d), (l)(e) and (l)(f), the reference to the rights of young persons is repeated. Mr. Speaker, all my studies in law were predicated upon the basic principle that every right had a corresponding duty. 1 have the right of ownership of property, but I have a duty not to use my property to the detriment of my neighbour.
I have an absolute right to my life, but I have a duty not to injure my neighbour. All the way through, there is no right without a corresponding duty.
There has been mention of a charter of rights to be included in the new Constitution. I was particularly struck by the absence of any mention of duties or obligations in that; it is all take and no give. In this particular instance too, every one of the rights that those young people have, carries a corresponding duty, and those duties should be included in the bill. To that extent I would say that clause 3 of the bill should be revised.
The parliamentary secretary spoke of some difficulties in recognizing the principle of vicarious liability and suggested that this was introducing the question of civil liability into criminal law. I believe that a young offender is not necessarily there; there are some nine, ten and II-year-olds who are the greatest little vandals you could meet. This brings up the question of the vicarious liability of parents.
If parents are so negligent in the care of their children and in giving them guidance that nine and ten-year-olds, and sometimes children younger than that, will break into schools and homes and vandalize them, then let the parents be responsible. We would see a lot of dressing up then. This may be a little old fashioned but I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that parents would shape up a lot better. There is no excuse when parents tootle off to the beer parlour or the tavern and leave the kids running the streets until ten or eleven o'clock at night, as we often see nine or ten-year-olds doing. If those parent were responsible and were held responsible and were not allowed to come crying, as we see on television, like sob sisters about their darling little kids, those mischievous little kids who do not mean any harm, things would be different. What would happen if those parents had to face up to the music of liability for the harm those children have done? Why is it that the victim, the defenceless public, the man whose car was legitimately parked outside his friend's house who comes out and finds it vandalized is the one who has to pay? And if it is the neighbourhood ten-year-old who has done that, why shouldn't the parents of the kid who is responsible be the one who should have to pay? Why should the victim suffer? Are we afraid of the words discipline, obedience and good conduct? Those are bad words in today's lexicon. We are told that we will set off repressions in children. It seems to me that we have to look at that too within a young offenders bill.

I think this bill does make considerable progress, but I do not think it makes enough. As I have said, I think more money should be put right across the board into the provision of supervisory social workers. If you do not want to call them parole officers, you can find any other words you like, but they should be the ones who will take in hand a far greater volume of young first offenders. These young first offenders should be segregated from older criminals. In the appropriate cases where we find vicious young thugs, then they should be treated in adult court. There are no two ways about it. We have to look to the protection of society. The state has a duty toward its citizens. Citizens have a right to live their peaceful lives uninjured. It is not a hazard of my life that I must run the risk of being robbed, of being mugged, of my life being taken or having my property being vandalized. That is not the role of our citizens. It is the duty of the state to protect them. It is the duty of the remaining citizens not to inflict those damages upon their fellow citizens.
I hope this bill will receive further attention in committee. I hope that the government's mind is open to amendments. The bill has taken a long time getting here. There have been changes. I hope the government can be flexible enough to accept suggestions that will improve the bill. After all, with whom are we dealing? We are dealing with people who are valuable to us, namely, our young people.
I used to think I was a lot more valuable when I was a young person than I am now. But surely this is something we, as legislators, must think about. We must not shut our minds to the fact that because the government has produced a bill, that is the end of the story in so far as sagacity and wisdom are concerned. We should never think because a bill is produced, it is the end of the story. No one loses face by accepting amendments. Not at all. I think one only betrays intelligence by doing so.
I would like to see this bill either deal generally with young offenders under age 16, or that we leave the option open so that those provinces who are, to my mind, enlightened enough to proceed on that basis of the younger age for young offenders may do so without any difficulty.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. My colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) tells me 1 have five minutes. I will do the very best I can to accommodate that time limitation.
First I want to recognize some people who work very hard in the family and youth field in the Hamilton area. I have long admired the work that they do. There are two who come to mind, and although I may miss others, I do not intend to offend them by not mentioning them. Both Judge Steinberg and Judge Van Duzer in Hamilton have devoted a lifetime to family and juvenile matters. They have been recognized over the years as having made substantial contributions. They have been innovative and understanding. In dealing with young
Young Offenders Act
offenders, in particular, that surely must be the way we should approach any misdemeanor or criminal act that is undertaken.
The subject of young offenders is a very puzzling topic. I want to say at the beginning that this legislation can be supported. I am not arguing against the legislation but I am expessing a frustration over how one deals with a topic which has so many different facets to it and a topic which has to take into account so many different circumstances. Dealing with young offenders is a very delicate matter in most cases.
Let us be fair about this. We are speaking about a small minority of young people. By far the vast majority are good, hard working, sensible, reasonable young people who grow up to be just like we are-whatever that is. However, even among the small minority who fall into the category of young offenders, there is an overwhelming majority of them, too, who break the law once and who then recognize the folly of it and go on to live useful and constructive lives.
What we are doing is trying to write a law, presumably to accommodate that majority of the minority, and at the same time write a law which will enable us to deal with the smaller minority who may turn out, as years pass, truly to become criminals of one kind or another. That almost defies logic.
I want to talk now about parents. Much of the responsibility for the way a child grows up must always remain in the lap or the hand of the parent involved. You cannot be the type of parent who rolls into the driveway dead drunk but expects his child will not drink and drive or suffer the attendant consequences thereof. You cannot constantly berate the police inside your home and on the streets and then expect your child to grow up to respect and support law enforcement and understand the difficulties encountered by the people in that line of work, a difficult line of work at the best of times. You cannot beat and physically abuse children or, for that matter, children and adults in the home, and expect that, by some mystical, magical means a child will be able to differentiate between that method of admonition-the commonly used method within their own home-and what is acceptable in society outside when they have to deal with other children. If violence is the order of the day in a child's home, then violence will be the order of the day outside for that child. When that child is met with frustration, he will respond in the same way as his parents respond. You cannot move into a new subdivision and decide you need a roll of tarpaper or some wood to build a rec room and just nip out the back door in the dead of night, pick it up and expect that your children will appreciate that somehow this is not stealing and, therefore, they ought not to do such things. You cannot plead for leniency when for years you have known that your child was bordering on anti-social behaviour, when finally the chickens come home to roost, so to speak. You cannot go in teary-eyed and ask that you not be held responsible in one way or another for the fact that you did nothing to try to change the anti-social behaviour the child was showing.

I think we all have to accept as parents and people in the community that we have a joint responsibility in the raising of children. We have to accept that the parents have a substantial responsibility, but the rest of us in the community also have a responsibility in the raising of children. We all have to show by example, by effort, by word, by deed and by involvement the kind of guidance that will allow those children to see that society can only survive if we all attempt to live within the law, and if the law is not just, you change it, you do not go around breaking it. I have always been concerned that we have not been able to instil in our own society the kind of sense that children belong to all of us, and that while we may have the child physically or adopt the child, the child is a child of all of us, and we all have to be cautions and careful.
Let me say that there are a number of factors in my judgment that influence a child's behaviour. I do not think it is nearly good enough to intrude yourself into the life of a child after the child becomes a teenager. Respect for an understanding of the law and the parameters that are allowed for behaviour within society are things which begin in the very earliest years, and from that point on a child learns what the rules are, how they are made and how they are changed, and that society is a democratic place and we change our rules in a democratic way. We do not go charging up to the Speaker screaming at him, for example, when we do not like what he does.
One of the things that is most influential in a child's behaviour is peer pressure, and, since children spend most of their time with other children during their school years, it is that arena to which we have to devote a considerable amount of time and money to make sure there are people there who are able to provide the kind of individual guidance children require. This is obvious, as I say, since they spend a great deal of time there. We must try to break down the unacceptable peer pressures and replace them with acceptable and useful peer pressures. We must hold up as examples people who have done useful and worth-while things as opposed to people who have lived on the fringe of the law.
I am not putting these in any particular order, but I think another important thing is parental guidance. I have mentioned that. There has to be an example set by all of us, both in the school and in the community, to make sure that the rewards that are given out, are given, and the recognitions that are made, are made for things that have been seen to be good things in society. We must stress the worth-while things while downplaying the others.
Let me say a word or two about jails and correctional institutions. My experience over a number of years has been that in correctional institutions in particular, since I do not have quite the experience in jails, the subculture from which the child comes to that correctional institution exists within the correctional institution. There is no doubt in my mind, borne out of any number of examples, that there is a subculture within the correctional institutions which inflicts and imposes the kinds of pressures which are the very opposite
pressures to those we would like to see for rehabilitation. It is for that reason in a way that I want-and I meant to do it at the beginning-to commend the member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) for his comments. I thought he made excellent sense. He showed by example in his own community the kind of work that can and should be done in every community all across the country. I hope copies of his remarks will be made available, and I know they are available, of course, in order that we can perhaps encourage that sort of thing to happen all across the country. I think it is in that area that we are likely to make the greatest strides and have the most success.
I do not want to downplay the fact that there is a growing violence in the community both at the adult and juvenile levels which is totally unacceptable. I want to say it is for me, and I am sure for most members of Parliament, a source of considerable worry how to deal with this growth of violence for its own sake. What do you do about it? Obviously the people involved have no particular fear. They generally organize themselves into groups and terrorize other people. I think we are going to have to devote more of our time and effort to infiltrating, if you will, those communities in an effort to try to break that up before it reaches the point where these people end up in Kingston, if it lasts, or some other institution.
I see my colleague looking over his shoulder at me. I have two minutes left. I was thinking about violence, and not only about violence committed by children but also about violence to children. Violence to children comes in many forms. Violence to children can be neglect, and violence to children can and is increasingly more apparently taking the form of incest and brutality. I think on balance society has not yet wakened up to this fact. The House of Commons might, at some more appropriate time, set aside some time to look at what I am sure may not be a new phenomenon, but certainly this phenomenon is coming more and more to the fore.
I do not want to leave the impression that I do not know or think that organizations which are offsprings of organized crime do not make themselves known to and involve themselves in the affairs of young people. The entire distribution for soft drugs is structured through the upper levels of organized crime, working its way down through a number of clearly visible organizations into the playgrounds, hallways and front yards of the schools, at least in the area I represent, and I think probably in many others. Young people are drawn in by the lure of money and the little bit of power they get. Once in they cannot get out because they do not know how to break away.
We have to support efforts to undermine that, get them out of there so we do not have a further deterioration of that growing up process which will hopefully turn out a better place and society in which to live.
In any event, to keep it brief, I say simply this. I want to stress that this can only be the beginning of the debate. This must be an ongoing debate. We will have to isolate many of the facets of juvenile misbehaviour and juvenile anti-social behaviour and of the pressures which are put on some people who are considerably younger than we, and we will have to
May 15, 1981

provide support in society so that we can try to cope with this because it is not good enough to say that if we just give them all a good whipping, they will suddenly respond positively. We used to do that, but we still had crime.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while this piece of legislation seems to deal with a narrow subject, it actually speaks to the larger question of our society, our values, our family life, some of the things which are closest to hon. members, and the way in which we transmit values to the next generation. I think that is why this debate has provoked a number of speeches. We just heard a good one from the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans).
I will start by indicating my support for the amendment introduced by my colleague, the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence). This is an important piece of legislation dealing with young offenders. The many amendments contained in this bill, among other things, actually repeal the Juvenile Delinquents Act. If we have to have as a cornerstone of the new act a variation in the maximum age across Canada, that is not acceptable.
That is not to say that most of what is found in Bill C-61 is not acceptable, for it is. It is well known that our party launched a similar process of legislation. Many of the points in Bill C-61 are what we ourselves advanced, so our quarrel is confined.
However, speaking as a member of Parliament from Alberta, I must say that I find it hard to understand why the government is proceeding on a piece of legislation which will allow for a diversity of the maximum age among young offenders. It is hard to understand why we have not waited until we could secure provincial agreement. Is it a question of money? Is it a question of philosophy? I do not believe this problem is insurmountable. I cannot understand why we are proceeding with such haste to bring in a law which will permit someone to be tried under the proposed Young Offenders Act in one province at age 16 and in another at age 17.
I am not particularly concerned about which age should be the maximum. I believe the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) was correct when he said that a person of age 16 today has sufficient maturity, given the over-all rapid maturation of young people today. I would hold to the age of 16, but I could live with the age of 17. Indeed, if it were the wisdom of the House to set the age at 18, I could live with that too. What I cannot live with is a variation from province to province.
If the government felt free to impose a charter of rights on all provinces regardless of provincial feelings-which have been made clear, and they are a source of great contention and controversy in the country, as we know-what is holding the government back from saying we will have a piece of legislation which will set a uniform age for young offenders across the country? That is the beginning of my approach to this subject.
Young Offenders Act
I want to make two or three other points, if I may, in the brief time remaining this afternoon. First, I think we ought to take just a second to underline a point which needs to be underlined now after a debate centring on young offenders, as if all young people were offenders and we had to spend an inordinate amount of time dealing with the offences of the young. In fact, most young people today are individuals in whom all of us should have immense pride. I certainly do. We should be proud of the way young people today are coping with the level of frustration in our society and with all those factors which are wrapped up in the phrase "future shock". We should be proud of the way they are coping.
I have five children of my own, and I try to stay close to young people, as close as an aging man can. Only this week two groups of young people came to Parliament Hill. One group was made up of the young people chosen for the program "Adventures in Citizenship" sponsored by the Rotary Club. I believe you yourself, Sir, participated in meeting them. The second group was made up of students brought here by the Commonwealth association from across Canada. They may be special students, to be sure, but to my mind-and I met both groups-they represented young people in whose values we ought to take great pride. We ought to give them a little boost and not create the impression that all young people need to be put into the category of young offenders.
When we do talk about young offenders, we cannot be naive and just slide over the fact that offences by juveniles are increasing. We have to live with that. That is a sad comment on our society, but it illustrates the need for a comprehensive piece of legislation. It places on such legislation a special imperative today. Senator Florence Bird recently said the following:
What is particularly scary-
Senator Bird was speaking about violent crime statistics in Canada.
-is the 60 per cent increase in violent juvenile delinquency from 1974 to 1978. Most shocking of all is the increase of violence by the young against themselves. In the past decade the suicide rate increased 59 per cent for young people aged 15 to 19.
That is just one indication of the need to take a good hard look at the best ways for society to handle young people, who for one reason or another, find themselves in trouble with the law. I want to return in a moment to some of the reasons for this, which ought to be at the real heart of this debate. We have to look at some of the reasons why young people find themselves in trouble with the law.
Bill C-61 deserves some praise, even though we are opposing the aspect of it which does not provide for uniformity of the maximum age among young offenders. The legislation blends three important principles. The first is that young people should be held responsible for their behaviour but not wholly accountable, since they are not fully mature. Second, society has the right to protection from illegal behaviour. Third, young people have the same right to due process of law and fair and equal treatment as adults. These rights must be guaranteed by special safeguards.

May 15, 1981
Young Offenders Act
Bill C-61 is a rather long piece of legislation, but that quick overview demonstrates why on the whole the bill merits the support of hon. members on all sides of the House.
We would be remiss if we did not look more deeply at the situation of young people in trouble with the law rather than just looking at how we are going to deal with them more effectively. It is the old question of whether to apply band-aid treatment or to get at the cause of the disease. Bill C-61 is more than a band-aid. Perhaps it is not able to do so, but it does not go deeply into the causes of crime by young offenders.
I believe we have to look into this much more deeply. If we spend a little while in this debate and if the committee is able to call witnesses who can speak to the causes, we will be performing a service not only for the parliamentary process, but for all Canadians.
The reason I take this tack in my contribution to this debate was that I recently saw a report of the Carnegie Council on Children. The council said the following:
Today virtually the last question we ask of any public policy is how it will affect children. It should become the first question.
Who speaks for the family today in the legislative halls? Young families have the least time, energy or financial resources to organize and make their voices heard. Indeed, how can they be self-sufficient when they are so deeply influenced by broad social and economic forces over which they have little control; unemployment, inflation, advertising, television, increased housing costs and inferior education systems. There is a whole range of factors that come into the spotlight when we start to look at the question of a family life that spawns for good or bad children who grow up in an atmosphere where they are loved and cared for or in families which allow undue influence from the outside, factors that hurt the transmission of true family values. I will speak of one of those in a moment.
If we are really serious about the problems of children who get into trouble with the law, we have to look collectively at such factors as child abuse statistics, the mental health picture, the divorce rate, the reasons for teenage suicide, the results of the Senate's examination of the relationship between crime and the criminal's early years. All of this helps us to have a growing knowledge of the character and personality development in the early years. When I speak about the early years, I want to talk about something I have come to learn in my life. I now see it reflected in many professional journals in the field of social sciences.
The most crucial period in the life of a human being is between the ages of three and five. That is when the whole
range of factors that give the person a sense of self-esteem need special attention. This is usually when the parents themselves are feeling the strongest pressures of a competitive society. The father is often totally immersed in the economic circumstances of his family. Often he is transferred. The family moves. We have a kind of tradition that as long as the child gets enough to eat and there is no manifest abuse or something terribly wrong such as a disease and ill-treatment, no one worries about it.
The fact is that survival is not enough. Many of the young people at whom this bill is aimed become young offenders because of an earlier period in their life when all they did was survive. A stable and secure atmosphere for children ought to have a top priority. Many aspects of our disjointed society come into play here. That is why the Carnegie Council on Children said that when we make public policies, the last thing we seem to think of is their effect on children.
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) is very conscious of the future aspects of the policy of his government. He would probably agree with what I am saying. When we look at questions of the environment, we are trying to protect all the physical manifestations of society for future generations. He has to have his mind on the future.
I hope that that example of the environment will be seen more widely in all of our policies, particularly our economic and social policies. I fear they are not. More attention ought to be paid to daycare and the provision of services for single parent families. In most single parent families, it is often the mother who has the responsibility. However, there are a growing number of instances where it is the father. They need services as well. It is not just a question of providing services but a question of society understanding the need to highlight and accent much more the values of family life.
I said I had one particular concern about outside influences. If we did a study, we would find that the television which a lot of young offenders have seen over the years has contributed to the venom which is reflected in them by their criminal conduct. We make sure that a child drinks pure water. We have laws to that effect. Why do we not have the courage to force the television industry to stop putting garbage and poison into children's minds with the ceaseless parade of murders, violence and seduction as so-called entertainment? That is on the minds of many parents. Why do we not pay more serious attention to these kinds of factors that have unquestionably been an influence in the formation of an important minority of our young people who have become offenders. I just have a moment left, Mr. Speaker.
The deeper we go into the question of children, the bigger the problem appears. In fact, in an address on children's rights, Justice Marcel Trahan of the Social Welfare Court, Montreal, emphasized the human interplay between society, the family and the child. He said:
When we talk about reforming the law, when we condemn certain institutions, we must be prepared to rethink the entire system.
May 15, 1981

1 see you are anxious to move on to the next proceeding, Mr. Speaker. May 1 call it four o'clock?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: It being four o'clock, the House will now proceed to the consideration of private members' business as listed on today's order paper, namely, notices of motions, public bills and private bills.
Motions Nos. 33, 38 and 40 allowed to stand by unanimous consent.

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should amend its policy of August 8, 1973, respecting the negotiation and settlement of all Indian, Inuit and Metis claims based on the traditional use and occupancy of land and any other aboriginal right not specifically extinguished by legitimate treaty or agreement, and in particular, to delete from the policy that condition that it will not negotiate claims superseded by law.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this motion is to amend, improve and correct the government's present policy for negotiating and settling native claims.
According to the present policy of the government adopted by a cabinet decision on August 8, 1973, the government will negotiate and settle claims according to the policy in the annual report of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development which can be found elsewhere as well. It indicates that the government will negotiate settlements with the Inuit and Indian people who have not entered into treaty relationships with the Crown and that these settlements would be based on the loss of their traditional use and occupancy of land in those parts of Canada where any native rights based on traditional use and occupancy have not been extinguished by treaty or superseded by law.
As far as I and many others who have worked in this field can see, there are three failings in that policy which my motion strives to correct. First, according to the policy, the government will only negotiate and settle claims based on land and the occupancy of land. As many hon. members know, aboriginal rights go much beyond the use and occupancy of land. During the lengthy sittings of the constitutional committee, we asked various Indian, Inuit and Metis groups what they meant
Native Claims
by aboriginal rights. Although they hesitated and in many cases refused to give an exact definition because they did not want to limit themselves, they indicated that aboriginal rights included not only land and the rights to hunt, fish and collect on those lands, but all their social, economic, political and cultural rights before the Europeans came which they never gave up. In other words, aboriginal rights include all the rights of those people before the Europeans came. They had societies, economies, languages and cultures. In some cases they hunted and fished; in other cases they raised crops and traded with other aboriginal peoples on the continent. They had a complete way of life. All those things are part of their aboriginal rights, to the extent that they have not given them up.
As I point out in my motion, I want to change the present policy of the government so that negotiations and settlements go much beyond land. In part, my motion reads:
-to the effect that it will negotiate settlement of all Indian, Inuit and Metis claims based on the traditional use and occupancy of land and any other aboriginal right-
So I want to include all aboriginal rights in the negotiations and settlements which will be concluded. That is the first goal of my motion. It is based upon the first failing of the present policy.
The second failing of the present policy is that it indicates that the government will negotiate the loss of traditional use and occupancy of land where these rights were based on traditional use and occupancy which have not been extinguished by treaty. What happened and what is still happening today is that when the government negotiates a land claim settlement with Inuit or Indian groups, it insists aboriginal groups give up all their rights, any rights they may have had in the past or will have in the future of which they may not be aware at the time. They want them to extinguish all their rights, not just the rights which they are giving up in the treaty or in the settlement in exchange for other rights, which is the way it should be. They want them to extinguish any potential or possible right whatsoever. I say that is wrong. In my motion I have suggested the policy should be that they settle "claims based on the traditional use and occupancy of the land and any other aboriginal right not specifically extinguished by legitimate treaty or agreement."
In other words, a right would only be extinguished if it was specifically referred to in the treaty or in the settlement agreement and if the Indians themselves agreed to extinguish that particular right in exchange for another right. That was the second failing I attempted to correct in my motion.
The third failing is the most shameful condition. Presently the government indicates that it will only negotiate and settle claims which have not been superseded by law. The government is saying that even if, from time immemorial, certain Indian or Inuit groups had aboriginal rights in certain parts of Canada, if a federal or provincial government passed a law of its parliament or legislature which took away those rights, then they are taken away and the government will not negotiate them.

May 15, 1981
Native Claims
This was the basis upon which the aboriginal claim of the Nova Scotia Indians was rejected by the office of native claims. They made a claim for certain lands, certain hunting and fishing rights, and certain other rights in Nova Scotia, Cape Breton and elsewhere. The government indicated that the government of Nova Scotia had passed statutes in various years and that the Government of Canada had passed other statutes in various years which divided the land into townships and took control of it. They had passed hunting and fishing laws and mineral rights laws, so they had exercised jurisdiction over the land. Despite what is right in principle and in justice, the government is saying that if a majority in a parliament or legislature passes a law that a right does not exist, it does not exist. Of course legally that might be correct, but morally it certainly is not. So in my motion I indicate that the government should remove entirely from its policy of negotiating and settling claims this business that it will not negotiate claims where they have been superseded by law, because I think it is wrong.
I drafted my particular motion last summer or fall before we became involved in the constitutional discussions and before the constitutional proposals were tabled in the House. This was well before what I believe to have been a historic day in January when, on the initiation of the government, after much lobbying by Indian and Inuit groups in this country, the government and all the parties sitting on the constitutional committee agreed to that section, part II, "Rights of the Aboriginal Peoples of Canada". Section 34(1) under that part reads:
The aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed.
By putting that section into the Constitution, much of my motion will no longer be necessary since later on in the constitutional proposal section 59(1) says:
The Constitution of Canada is the supreme law of Canada, and any law that is inconsistent with the provisions of the Constitution is, to the extent of the inconsistency, of no force or effect.
This means that once the provision is passed by this House and by the British Parliament, which I hope will happen soon, the land claims settlement policy of the government will be, to a great extent, of no force or effect in accordance with section 59(1). It will have no force or effect because the laws which are referred to in the policy which superseded these claims are ordinary laws of the Parliament of Canada and ordinary laws of the legislatures of the provinces. Because they are ordinary laws, they give way to whatever is in these constitutional proposals. Since in these constitutional proposals we have a recognition of aboriginal and treaty rights, they will prevail over any cities and towns act any provincial fish and game act, any provincial mining act, any federal oil and gas act or any national energy board act which are all ordinary laws. So once the aboriginal group, whether it be Indian, Inuit or Metis, reaches agreement by negotiation with the government, or through the courts if the government will not settle with them, then those rights prevail over any policy of the government
with respect to claims. Consequently, it is my belief that this policy which I am attempting to amend, improve and change through my motion, will fall down completely once the Constitution is adopted in Britain.
I would like to deal with a recent case where the National Energy Board approved the construction of a pipeline from Norman Wells in the Northwest Territories up the McKenzie River to the Alberta border and through Alberta. The Board approved this pipeline over territories which are claimed to be part of the territory of the Dene. The Dene have claimed much of that land as theirs in accordance with their aboriginal rights. Without this constitutional proposal, the government might say that, because of the National Energy Board Act and its decision, that is a statute of Parliament and that it is a legal decision of the National Energy Board. They may say that it would prevail over the rights of the Dene, if they wanted to rest their case on purely legal grounds. But with the passage of this section it is my belief, as a trained lawyer, that this constitutional provision will prevail over any decision of the National Energy Board, and as section 59 (1) says "any law that is inconsistent with the provisions of the Constitution is, to the extent of the inconsistency, of no force or effect."
Although I prepared this motion to correct the three failings I referred to in the negotiation of our native claims policy, I still wish it were done by the government on a voluntary, unilateral basis. Even though it may not be done today, the provisions in the constitutional proposal will do it in any case. Even if the constitutional proposal is passed this year, I hope that the government will not force our native people to test these matters in the courts in order to resolve them, that it will not put them to considerable expense in terms of time and money. Who knows, matters like this can take two, three, four or five years to go through the whole court system. The government agreed to put these provisions in the Constitution. I believe it did so with good will and it was supported by all parties on the constitutional committee. Therefore, it is my belief that the government should voluntarily change right away the provisions of this policy for negotiating claims. It should not wait until the court forces changes to the policy.
This week in the Indian Affairs and Northern Development Committee I asked the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) if he had set up a small group within his department to determine what the effects the new constitutional proposals relating to aboriginal and treaty rights would have on all the laws, regulations and policies which he administers. He said that he had set up such a small group under one of his assistant deputy ministers and that they were attempting to determine where the laws they administered were ultra vires or of no force and effect. He said he believed that it was right that they should not put ordinary citizens of native groups to great expense in the courts. He said that where it was clear that their laws and policies were ultra vires, they should be changed by immediate agreement, or as soon as the constitutional proposal is passed.
My main point in presenting this motion was to correct the failings and inadequacies in our present policy for negotiating
May 15, 1981

claims with our native people in this country. 1 said that the present policy was wanting in that it only dealt with land and matters related to land, for example, hunting and fishing. I said that it did not deal with the wide range of aboriginal rights. Second, it insisted on complete extinguishment when that was not really necessary or fair. Third, a claim would not even be considered if it were felt that it had been superseded by some ordinary provincial or federal law. All of these failings should go. They should go on the basis of justice and moral right. But since the governemnt has agreed to the provision which it has placed in its constitution proposals, I think that in virtue of that provision they will go. I ask the government to give immediate attention to my submissions. I certainly would be pleased if the government would agree to this motion today.

subsubtopic: POLICY RESPECTING NEGOTIATION AND SETTLEMENT OF NATIVE CLAIMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on this matter because it illustrates one of the causes of concern of our native people. I have in my hand a copy of Indian News for April, 1981, put out under the Indian and Inuit Affairs program. The heading there is "Bill C-48 snuffs Aboriginal Rights". I want to deal with some of the points which are certainly of concern to the editor of this paper who is speaking for a large number of people. But before doing that, I would suggest that if the government is really sincere in its desire to give aboriginal treaty rights to our Indian people, it should withdraw the legislation which is in conflict with that particular section.
The hon. member who just spoke has given three very definite items which are in conflict, in my view, with part 2 of the proposed Constitution. One of the things which has bothered me throughout this constitutional talk is that we are raising the hopes of people without even defining what the aboriginal treaty rights are. When that is done, the whole matter could be involved in weeks, months or years of litigation. When Indian or native people have to compete against the government, the largest corporation in the country, with relation to lawyers and paying for the costs arising out of litigation, then it does not give people an equal chance even though we say they are equal. They certainly are not.
In Section 33, the proposed Constitution says, "the aboriginal treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed", but it does not say what they are. Is it the aboriginal right to own land? Is it their aboriginal right to social life? Is it their aboriginal rights to learning, hunting, fishing, or carrying out their own economics as they did before the white man came? No one knows. So no wonder our native people are concerned about this, because when it does not say what it is specifically, then we can hope all we like but it will go to the courts. There will be conflicts, it will go to the courts and then it will be ruled on by those who are sitting on the bench.
Again, in subsection 2 of this act, it says, "Aboriginal peoples of Canada includes the Indian, Inuit and Metis peoples of Canada." It states there who is included; but it does not say
Native Claims
what the rights are. That is one of my major objections to this. If this is put in simply to appease our native people at this time, then it is a terrible thing indeed. It would be trickery of the worst kind if that is the objective. If that is not the objective, the government should show its good faith now by withdrawing at least legislation which is in conflict with those aboriginal and treaty rights.
I again agreed that these should not be confined only to land. The aboriginal people lived on this continent long before we did. We say that they were conquered. Maybe they were conquered by kind words and by arrangements rather than through actual warfare, although there may have been some warfare too. However, they were guaranteed, as long as the waters run and as long as the sun shines, rights that they had before the white man came.
Now, the government has set out in its policy at least three rights. Referring to the one on land, it is not only land which is involved with relation to aboriginal rights, as the last hon. member to speak so aptly said. The second right as spelled out is even worse. It says, "Not extinguished by treaty or agreement". "Treaty or agreement", again is not defined. We celebrated the 100th year of Treaty Seven out on the plains of the Blackfoot just a couple of years ago. The Prince of Wales was there and so were ministers from provincial and federal governments. It was a tremendous "do". The Indians came from far and wide. There was a great celebration on the very plains where the treaty was signed. However, would we have to tell them, if this Constitution becomes law, that they have their rights in the Constitution, but that the policy which was on the books before is still on the books, and that it extinguishes their rights because their forefathers signed the treaty? These are the worries of our native people.
The third one is even more serious. It states: "superseded by law". Already, since we put the provision in the Constitution guaranteeing the aboriginal treaty rights, we are taking their rights away by law. Look at Bill C-48. As the editor of this Indian News says, "Bill C-48 snuffs Aboriginal Rights". Let us just read one or two items from this particular article, and I quote:
The bill has no environmental protection worthy of the name. In fact, in environmental terms, it may well be the weakest single statute of its kind ever to come before the Parliament of Canada.
The environment is almost an Indian's whole life. The Indians live amongst the trees, they live with the animals, they learn from the animals. They have a closer kinship with nature than the white men have ever had and they want to retain it. Then the story goes on as follows:
The bill implicitly extinguishes-
Notice the word "extinguishes".
-Aboriginal Rights by utterly ignoring them. So-called Canada Lands in the Territories are in reality Aboriginal Lands. The Bill extinguishes precisely those rights which the Charter of Rights pretends to guarantee.
So, even before the Constitution becomes law, we are passing other laws and taking away the rights that we are leading native people to believe they will have if and when the proposed Constitution becomes the Constitution of Canada.

May 15, 1981
Native Claims

speechtext:
1 would like to read one other passage from this story:
The Bill jeopardizes any coherent evolution toward responsible government by taking away in advance the access to resource revenues-which would constitute the fiscal base for such a government and secondly, it makes a mockery of the aboriginal claims process by pre-empting all resource revenues for the federal government.
It has been said that if one wants to make an independent man a slave, one deprives him of his bread and his water, and that when he gets hungry enough, he will sell his rights for bread and water in order to survive. Some will and some will not; but a great number will. Here we have a section in Bill C-48 which says that the natural resources are going to belong to the federal government, denying for all time the chance of our aboriginal people in that part of our country to ever become an independent people with a buoyant economy. We take away their means of becoming a buoyant citizenry which could be proud and make a contribution to the country.
I think the government now has a chance to show whether it is sincere in putting this section in the bill about aboriginal rights. A few weeks before it was inserted in the bill, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said in this House something to the effect that, "If you will tell me what aboriginal rights are I will agree or disagree." A few weeks after that, the clause was put in without those rights being defined in any way.
As an individual I support the bill, Mr. Speaker. If the government is sincere in its desire to be fair with the native people in regard to aboriginal rights, it should show its hand by withdrawing the policy we are discussing today.

subsubtopic: POLICY RESPECTING NEGOTIATION AND SETTLEMENT OF NATIVE CLAIMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should also like to speak to the motion proposed by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) and to commend the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) for his comments.
From our perspective, this policy on land claims is somewhat anachronistic in light of the recent constitutional steps taken by Parliament as a whole.
After eight years, the 1973 land claims policy is a document which is outmoded in the context of the recent constitutional recognition of aboriginal rights.
The 1973 policy required the extinguishment of "native interest" in certain lands in exchange for some kind of compensation. It further limited negotiations only to areas where native title had never been extinguished by treaty or superseded by law.
The policy's provisions had the effect of smoothing the way for resource developers in the north by extinguishing aboriginal title, and in the south by precluding negotiations in areas where resource developers were already established.
The kind of settlement this policy offered native people was loss of political and economic control in exchange for their assuming full responsibility for their own well-being.
In a paper on the 1973 policy statement on native settlements, Murray Angus discusses the advantages of this policy for the federal government. He says:
The type of compensation, particularly the large cash payments, served to legitimate the government's over-all handling of the native problem and also exonerated it from much of the responsibility for their future welfare.
The problems with implementation of the James Bay agreement-with all due respect to James Bay Inuit and Indians- demonstrates quite clearly how the federal government abrogates responsibility in native communities after it has reached a "compensation for extinguishment" settlement, as was the case in the James Bay agreement.
The 1973 policy also had the effect of moving questions of aboriginal title out of the courts in order to facilitate the negotiations process. Even though court cases are time-consuming and costly, native people have demonstrated over and over that they are patient. This was very evident in the Baker Lake court case. Perhaps it is fair to say that federal government and resource developers are not patient, but there has been increasing pressure to settle "claims" in order to speed up development. Bill C-48 is such an exercise.
The reformed Constitution which recognizes and affirms aboriginal rights and aboriginal title, has important implications for the settlement of comprehensive claims. Constitutional rights cannot be extinguished by any legislation or policy statement. Everyone knows that the idea of extinguishment is not only anachronistic, but will shortly be legally impossible.
Comprehensive claims are not simply a way "to remove the sense of grievance and injustice which impedes the relationship of the Indian and Inuit peoples with the governments concerned and with their fellow Canadians," as the 1973 policy statement suggests. Comprehensive claims provide a mechanism for defining aboriginal rights for the first time in Canadian history.
The present policy, based on the 1973 policy statement, prejudices the process of defining rights through comprehensive claims negotiations. For example, the present policy prohibits negotiations on land which contains oil and gas reserves. This certainly prejudges the issue of whether aboriginal title includes rights to oil and gas benefits on land subject to aboriginal title. We know the value of the buck as well as anyone in Canada. It also explains the apprehension expressed by northerners about the proposed oil and gas act.
The Inuit Tapirisat of Canada and the federal government are now involved in comprehensive claims negotiations. It is not known, however, whether the Inuit Tapirisat can negotiate on those lands which contain oil and gas and on those lands on which Bill C-48 will increase development. Last summer the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada addressed the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I quote Thomas Suluk, the chief negotiator for the Inuit Tapirisat as follows:
May 15, 1981

A land claims settlement between the Inuit of Nunavut and the federal government should reflect an awareness that the days of trinkets and tiny reserves are over; an awareness that a people cannot retain its self-reliance and self-esteem if the power to shape its future is appropriated by others.
Implicit in this statement is the realization that for Inuit, land claims negotiations and political development issues are inseparable. Self-reliance and self-esteem do not result from transfers of money, but rather from the management of one's own affairs within the greater society in a way which integrates the cultural pride of a people with political and economic structures responsive to the people.
The Inuit of Nunavut have proposed the creation of a new Territory in the Eastern Arctic. The Nunavut territory is supported not only by those who, like their ancestors, were born in the north, but also by those who have chosen to make Nunavut their home. This includes many people from the south.
The legislative assembly of the Northwest Territories passed a number of resolutions last November which address the question of division of the territory. These resolutions include recognition of the present geo-political structure of the Northwest Territories as an interim arrangement and commitment in principle to the divsion of the Northwest Territories into eastern and western portions, subject to the expressed will of the people, by plebiscite.
In 1974, Dr. Lloyd Barber of Regina University, in his role as Indian Claims Commissioner for Canada at that time, stated, in relation to Dene rejection of the notion of "extinguishment" of aboriginal rights, as follows:
I cannot emphasize too strongly that we are in a new ball game. .. We've been allowed to delude ourselves about the situation for a long time because of a lack of political power in native communities.
Seven years after this statement was made, the constitutional package recognized and affirmed aboriginal rights. It has been a long and tough battle, and one which, in many ways, has only just begun. Perhaps the recent constitutional amendments are a beginning.
Political power in native communities may be growing. The evolution planned by the Northwest Territories government may reflect that. Perhaps this growth will foster changes in attitude among the politicians and bureaucrats who handle native claims.
We await with interest the forthcoming comprehensive policy of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) and we fully expect it to reflect the change in official government attitudes which the constitutional revision process began. I have spoken in support of the motion of the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East.
Some years ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated that he would never see the north attain provincial status. He also said there were no aboriginal rights. Perhaps his changed in attitude toward aboriginal people, with his commitment to constitutional recognition of those people will reflect changes in his attitude or political awareness of the north as well as of other parts of the country.
