speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) and thank him for his interest in the cause of the native people of Canada, not only in this House, but also in the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development, especially as the motion which he introduced today gives us an opportunity to review the situation of the native people of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, history tells us that several attempts have been made to meet more adequately the concerns of the Canadian native people. The federal government has recognized the validity of this objective. On August 8, 1973, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development announced the policy of the government concerning the claims of the Indians and Inuit.
On the one hand, this policy reaffirmed the principle long recognized by this government that legal obligations towards the Indians would be met; for this purpose, the government would continue to hear such grievances as the Indians might state concerning its administration of Indian lands and other property under the provisions of the Indian Act and Regulations, as well as such claims as might be made concerning the negotiation and interpretation of treaties with the Indian people or agreements and proclamations concerning the Indians and the reservations. In this statement of policy, Mr. Speaker, the claims based on these grievances were called particular claims.
On the other hand, the government of Canada stated that it was willing to negotiate the settlement of claims with native groups in the regions of Canada where, in keeping with traditional use or occupation of the land of these regions, these groups had acquired certain rights which had never been cancelled by a treaty or an act. While this interest was never conclusively recognized or defined in Canadian law, it ensues from the traditional utilization and occupation of lands in these regions, which include the Yukon, Northern Quebec, the major part of British Columbia and the Northwest Territories. The government recognized that occupation of these lands by non-Indians had not taken this right into account, that the Indians had not been offered compensation for the gradual erosion of their rights, and that generally, this had prevented the native people from taking advantage of the development which could have resulted from the settlement of these lands.
The claims which would be based on that principle are called "over-all claims". I think the summary I have just made of the policy concerning aboriginal rights in 1973 may be of some use. However, to appreciate its full import it would be advisable to read the statement made by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development on August 8, 1973. Several Indian bands in Canada Maintain relationships with the federal government which are symbolized in the treaties

May 15, 1981
Native Claims
they have made with the Crown in the course of history. Since the government committed itself a few years ago in the case of Indian claims and treaties, the legitimate rights of the Indians must be recognized. That still remains the basis of government policy.
The commitment of the government of Canada to abide by the treaties has been reaffirmed very recently by Her Majesty the Queen when she spoke to Alberta's Indian representatives in Calgary on July 5. Among other things, Her Majesty the Queen said, and I quote:
You may rest assured that the government of Canada acknowledges the significance of fully observing the treaties, both in the spirit and in the terms of those agreements.
That declaration and the present policy statement testify to the fact that pursuant to the provisions of the British North America Act, the government acknowledges and accepts its continuing responsibility for the Indians and the territories which have been reserved for them. In that respect the government considers that its position results from a historic evolution which dates back to the royal proclamation of 1763, which remains a fundamental declaration of the territorial rights of Indians in this country, regardless of the differences that may have surfaced in its legal interpretation.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, as a result of a court ruling, the jurisdiction of the federal government over the Indians has been extended so as to include the Eskimos and the Inuit. If we are again drafting new premises at this time it is because we want to point out that the ensuing policy statement is not meant to make amendments to it. The government wants to reaffirm to the native people involved and to the people of Canada generally that its policy in that respect is nothing less than an attestation of its responsibility.
This policy is concerned with the claims and the proposed settlements of already old grievances. Those claims originate from Indian bands which have not signed treaties with the Crown. According to them they are warranted under various titles: Indian title of ownership, title of aboriginal ownership, aboriginal title of ownership, native right of ownership or right of usufruct. Essentially, the native people seek to obtain compensation by filing claims based on the loss of traditional enjoyment and occupation of territories in certain parts of Canada where the property title of the Indians has never been abolished by treaty nor replaced by statute. Ever since it came to power in 1968 the government has accepted those claims and provided funds as well as other forms of assistance to the Indians and the Inuit so as to enable them to do the research necessary to establish their traditional territorial interests.
The government has now received official requests from certain native groups and knows that others will follow suit. The lands involved are in British Columbia, Northern Quebec, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. In reviewing its approach to Indian and Inuit claims, the government has
considered and taken into account the briefs presented by various associations and the opinions expressed both by those groups and the members of the Standing Committee on Indian and Northern Affairs, on which I sit as well as recent court proceedings dealing with Indian claims. The government is well aware of the fact that the claims do not involve mere land and money issues but that they are related to a way of life. Therefore, any settlement must, in a positive and durable way, help solve the cultural, social and economic problems which for far too long have maintained the Indians and Inuits as second-class citizens in our society.
Basically, the government's view is that these claims must be settled and that the best way to do so is through negotiations. These negotiations should result in agreements with the various Indian and Inuit groups involved and such agreements should be enshrined in legislation voted by this Parliament so as to have force of law. I heard the hon. member for Nunat-siaq (Mr. Ittinuar) of the Northwest Territories a moment ago express his pleasure at the fact that since aboriginal rights would be included in the Constitution the settlement of land claims would no doubt be speeded up, and I think that it is a credit to members of this House that they passed the amendment that was put forth during the constitutional debate.
Mr. Speaker, this government is now prepared to negotiate with the official spokesmen of these groups on the principle that if the traditional rights to the lands claimed can be established, native people will receive just compensation or benefit for these interests. The lands that are in litigation do not fall under federal jurisdiction. In the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, the government has the power to use Crown lands after consulting with the territorial governments. With respect to the claims involving lands in the provinces, provincial powers and the rights of Canadians living on those lands have to be so considered. So as to reach satisfactory agreements with the Indians and Inuit residing in the provinces, the latter, together with the federal government, must get involved in the negotiation and settlement process. It is in the interest of these provinces and their residents that these land claims be settled and it is reasonable to say that the provinces are prepared to offer compensation. The government has made its position clear to the provinces involved and has strongly urged them to participate in the proposed negotiations. There are differences between some of the native claims and other differences are bound to come up in the future. They stem mostly from the settlements that have been proposed and require a flexible approach which the government is willing to take.
About a year ago, the B.C. Indian Chiefs Union demanded compensation based on the traditional loss of enjoyment and land occupation in that province. Since then, the courts have answered the Nishga claims relating mostly to lands under provincial jurisdiction. The government is now ready to negoti-
May 15, 1981

ate those Indian claims in British Columbia and considers the provincial participation as essential to a satisfactory settlement.
As for New Quebec, most important legal cases related to Indian claims in that area are now before the provincial courts. Once again, the federal government believes that negotiation is the best method of obtaining the results hoped for by all parties concerned, and it will spare no effort to find a solution. However, as those questions are now before the courts, it would be improper for the Canadian government to say more on the matter.
The government has already agreed with the representatives of the Yukon Indians to start negotiations concerning their claims. Those dealing with the proposed settlement have already started. The government is also ready to negotiate with the associations of non-treaty Indians and Inuits from the Northwest Territories. The government has made clear for quite some time that it is willing to fully meet its obligations, show flexibility and hold consultations with the interested parties. Like the Indian groups of Canada, the Northwest Territories Eskimos have obtained funds to help them carry out studies on land claims. In all cases where it is acknowledged that traditional land interests have been disregarded, the government has been willing to look into them and it recognizes in principle the need to compensate any loss resulting from such neglect. It agrees that the best way to achieve the proposed objectives is to reach a freely negotiated settlement with all parties concerned.
Mr. Speaker, in some parts of the country, such as southern Quebec and the Atlantic provinces, there are no treaties dealing with transfer of lands. In this regard, the government is of the opinion that territorial claims in those areas are different in nature from those we spoke of a while ago. The Indians submitted claims concerning their interests in those
Native Claims
lands which the government is now in the process of studying. It has also provided them with funds to pursue their necessary research. The policy of the government with regard to the claims of our native peoples fits into the context of other policies intended to alleviate the feeling of bitterness and unfairness that dampens good relations between, on the one hand, the Indians and the Eskimos, and, on the other, the governments concerned and the other Canadians. I see, Mr. Speaker, it is almost five o'clock. Once again, I wish to say how pleased 1 was to take part in this debate.
This policy has been the mechanism used throughout the study of the claims mentioned by the first speaker. Now that it has been suggested that the rights of our native people be entrenched in our Constitution, the settlement of land claims will no doubt be speeded up. There is no reason to stop negotiations already under way for that purpose and wait for final patriation-
